articles.title: Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms
articles.summary: Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.
Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement.
Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.
Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.
During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”.
“The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said.
September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.
Warsh declined to comment on a remark from Donald Trump that, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”.
“I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said.
Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.
Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.
The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.
“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.
Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.
The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.
By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.
“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.
On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.

articles.title: US Fed FOMC pauses interest rates: Can Nifty bulls take charge or will RBI hike spoil the rally? Investors guide - Livemint
articles.summary: US Fed FOMC pauses interest rates: Can Nifty bulls take charge or will RBI hike spoil the rally? Investors guide  Livemint
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates unchanged has offered some support to Indian equities, but the relief may prove short-lived if domestic interest rates rise in the coming months.
Sensex jumped 762 points or 1% to the day's high of 74,007.70, while the broader Nifty 50 rose 210 points or 0.9% to an intra-day high of 22,908.75.
Emkay expects the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to deliver another 75 basis points of cumulative rate hikes in the current cycle, with increases anticipated in December 2026 and February 2027. This raises a key question for investors: can the Nifty sustain its gains amid the prospect of tighter domestic monetary policy, elevated crude oil prices and persistent inflationary pressures?
The Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to maintain the US federal funds target range at 3.75%-4%, following a rate hike at its September meeting. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation remained too high and indicated that policymakers needed more data before deciding on their next move. US consumer inflation stood at 3.7% in September.
Domestic brokerage Emkay believes the combination of elevated US interest rates, high oil prices and weak natural dollar inflows could push the RBI towards further monetary tightening. These factors could increase pressure on the rupee and raise India's risk premium, limiting the central bank's ability to look through global inflationary pressures.
The brokerage expects 75 basis points of cumulative rate hikes in the current cycle, including 25-basis-point increases in December 2026 and February 2027. Its assessment is based on the view that resilient domestic growth gives the RBI room to respond to inflation risks, while policymakers are likely to favour measured rather than aggressive tightening.
For equity investors, the prospect of higher interest rates could weigh on valuations, particularly in expensive market segments. Higher borrowing costs may also affect companies with significant debt or those whose earnings depend on strong consumer demand.
The Fed's decision to hold rates steady could provide temporary relief to emerging markets by reducing immediate concerns about further US monetary tightening. However, the outlook for Indian equities will also depend on the trajectory of US bond yields, the dollar, crude oil prices and foreign portfolio investment flows.
Ajitabh Bharti, co-founder and executive director of Capital XB, viewed the Fed's decision as supportive for India in the near term because a softer US policy stance could ease pressure on the rupee and stabilise capital flows. However, he questioned whether the decision adequately addressed persistent inflation risks.
"The Fed's latest decision has come across as notably dovish — and somewhat surprising, given that inflation continues to run well above target. Easing the policy stance at this stage carries a genuine risk that the central bank could lose control of price pressures just when credibility matters most," Bharti said.
He also warned that perceptions of political influence over monetary policy could undermine confidence in the dollar, creating uncertainty for global markets.
Thomas Priju, portfolio manager at Karma Capital, warned that rising US rates could create volatility in Indian equities by keeping bond yields and the dollar elevated. He also highlighted the vulnerability of high-valuation stocks and companies dependent on foreign portfolio flows.
“For Indian equities, the implications could be significant. A further increase in US interest rates could keep US bond yields and the dollar elevated, putting pressure on emerging-market capital flows and increasing volatility in the Nifty. High-valuation stocks and segments dependent on foreign portfolio flows could remain particularly sensitive to changes in global liquidity conditions,” said the brokerage.
Priju said investors should focus on businesses with strong earnings visibility and healthy balance sheets while monitoring US inflation data and the Fed's subsequent communication for clues about the interest-rate outlook.
“However, the impact on Indian markets will also depend on domestic earnings growth, valuations and the trajectory of foreign investor flows. Investors should remain selective and focus on companies with strong earnings visibility and balance sheets, while monitoring US inflation data and the Fed’s subsequent communication for clues on the future rate trajectory,” he added.
His assessment suggests that the Fed's rate decision alone may not be sufficient to sustain a market rally. Domestic earnings performance, valuations and foreign investor activity will remain important determinants of the Nifty's direction.

articles.title: With the Federal Reserve on pause and the Bank of Japan likely to hold steady, why does liquidity remain tight? December rate hike uncertainty rattles stocks, bonds, and currencies. - 富途牛牛
articles.summary: With the Federal Reserve on pause and the Bank of Japan likely to hold steady, why does liquidity remain tight? December rate hike uncertainty rattles stocks, bonds, and currencies.  富途牛牛
articles.full_text:
The market widely expects the Bank of Japan to hold its benchmark interest rate steady on Friday, while signaling that underlying inflation has finally reached its 2% target. A key question is whether the central bank will announce that, for the first time since setting the target in 2013, core inflation has broadly hit the 2% goal—a development that appears highly likely.
Zhitong Finance APP has learned that economists generally expect the Bank of Japan to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Friday, while noting that underlying inflation has finally reached and remained above its 2% target for an extended period. This milestone will strengthen the case for further rate hikes.
In a recent Bloomberg survey of economists worldwide, all respondents who have long monitored the Bank of Japan's policy trajectory expect the central bank to hold its policy rate steady at the conclusion of its two-day meeting this week. Last month, the Bank of Japan raised its key interest rate to 1.25%.
As shown in the chart above, the Bank of Japan under Kazuo Ueda is still steadily advancing its interest-rate hike process.
A key focus on Friday will be whether the Bank of Japan signals that underlying inflation has broadly reached its 2% target. This would be the first time since the target was set in 2013, and such an outcome appears quite likely. It would bolster the case for further interest-rate hikes, as Japan's borrowing costs remain relatively low and continue to provide a stimulus.
Ryutaro Kawano, Chief Economist for Japan at BNP Paribas, stated: "The Bank of Japan likely judges that underlying inflation has now reached around 2%. The central bank may believe it is necessary to raise interest rates to a neutral level as soon as reasonably feasible, but the upside risks to inflation are not yet sufficient to compel it to hike rates at two consecutive meetings."
Ahead of the Bank of Japan's meeting, the Federal Reserve left its policy settings unchanged overnight. The decision weighed on the U.S. dollar, pushing the yen to around 157.84 per dollar in Tokyo on Thursday morning.
Although the Bank of Japan has remained relatively vague about the true level of underlying inflation, numerous indicators have long suggested that inflation is taking root in Japan. In March this year, the Bank began publishing a new set of price measures designed to track changes in core inflation after stripping out factors that are largely temporary.
Raising the baseline inflation forecast will lay the groundwork for another interest-rate hike at the December meeting. More than 80% of surveyed economists expect the central bank to act then. In September, the Bank of Japan adjusted its policy rate, marking the second rate increase in three months and signaling the fastest pace of tightening in 36 years.
Sources told Bloomberg earlier this month that, given current price trends and the central bank's assessment that interest-rate hikes to date have had only limited impact on the economy, the Bank of Japan may continue raising rates at roughly the same pace.
Kazuo Ueda has increasingly stated that core inflation is "very close" to 2%, seemingly preparing investors for a shift in wording in Friday's quarterly outlook report. Earlier this month, he indicated that the Bank of Japan would not allow core inflation to rise significantly further from its current level.
Acknowledging that underlying inflation has already reached its target will prompt the market to focus more on how much further interest rates need to rise before policy ceases to be stimulative. The Bank of Japan estimates that the neutral rate lies between 1.1% and 2.5%, while emphasizing that it is difficult to determine precisely. Institutions such as JPMorgan Securities and BNP Paribas expect the terminal rate in this cycle to reach 2.5%.
The inflation gauge that excludes fresh food has long been a key metric of focus for the Bank of Japan. As of March this year, it has exceeded the central bank's target for four consecutive fiscal years; if the bank's latest projections prove accurate, it will have remained above target for six straight years. Some economists argue that the Bank of Japan has been overly cautious in acknowledging this shift, risking falling behind the curve in addressing inflation.
The above chart indicates that Japan's inflation is expected to remain above the Bank of Japan's 2% target. Note: All figures are annualized.
Kameida, a former economist at the Bank of Japan and currently an executive economist at Sompo Institute Plus, stated: "Five to six years is generally enough time for a first-grader to advance to junior high school. If someone were to claim that inflation persisting over this entire period still does not constitute a trend, it would be hard to imagine anyone accepting such a view."
Recent economic data, along with early signals ahead of next year's wage negotiations, indicate that inflationary pressures remain firm. Last month, a key measure of core inflation in Japan surged to 3.2%, the highest level in three years. Following three consecutive years of record‑high wage growth, Japan's largest trade union federation plans to seek even larger pay increases in the upcoming round of talks, which are expected to conclude with an agreement in March.
Taro Kimura, an economist at Bloomberg Economics, said: "Ahead of next year's annual wage negotiations, early signals from both labor and management leaders suggest that Japan's wage growth could accelerate in 2027. This could further fuel inflation and increase the risk that the Bank of Japan will raise its benchmark interest rate above the roughly 2% terminal level currently priced into the market."
The divergence among the Bank of Japan's nine policy board members over the inflation outlook was already reflected in last month's 7‑to‑2 vote. That outcome left the yen weaker even after the rate hike. Investors will be watching Friday's vote for signs of further momentum behind rate increases.
Reaching this milestone in the price‑level target would mark the culmination of a policy effort that began in 2013, when the Bank of Japan launched a massive monetary easing program aimed at achieving 2% inflation within roughly two years. However, Japan did not experience sustained price increases until nearly a decade later—driven in part by the global inflationary shock triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
In March 2024, as the Bank of Japan grew increasingly confident that its core inflation target was on track to be achieved, it ended the world's last negative interest rate policy and its yield curve control program. Kazuo Ueda has raised interest rates six times to date, marking the highest number of rate hikes by a single Bank of Japan governor in at least half a century.
In a recent podcast episode, former Deputy Governor Hiroshi Nakaso, who spent nearly four decades at the Bank of Japan, underscored this long-awaited economic shift. Prior to this, following the bursting of the asset bubble in the 1990s, Japan endured "the Lost Three Decades," during which roughly 200 financial institutions collapsed.
"Japan is back," said Hiroshi Nakaso. "Deflation has finally become a thing of the past, and the economy is shifting toward an inflationary regime."
However, achieving the target does not signify an unqualified success for inflation. While price increases have been accompanied by record corporate profits, nominal GDP, and tax revenues, they have also heightened concerns about the cost of living, particularly among Japan's rapidly aging population. Nearly 30 percent of Japanese citizens are aged 65 or older, and roughly 40 percent of elderly households rely entirely on pensions for their income.
Hiroshi Nakaso once stated that he would pop open a bottle of champagne to celebrate when the central bank achieves its price stability target. He emphasized that even after the Bank of Japan meets its goal, the government will still need to formulate a robust growth strategy.
Zhong Zenghong said, "This necessity has not diminished in the slightest."
The Bank of Japan's "hawkish pause" is imminent: the 2% inflation milestone continues to pave the way for the next steps in its rate-hike trajectory.
The most significant potential change at this Bank of Japan meeting is the first explicit acknowledgment that underlying inflation has broadly reached the 2% target, while maintaining the policy rate at 1.25%, thereby strengthening the rationale for continuing the exit from accommodative monetary policy.
Here, "underlying inflation" refers to the central bank's assessment of the persistent price trend after stripping out temporary factors; it is not equivalent to the consumer price index for any given month. Japan's inflation measure excluding fresh food has remained above 2% for several years, yet the central bank has continued to await stronger, sustained evidence from wage growth, service prices, and firms' pricing behavior. In a Bloomberg survey, all surveyed analysts expect a pause this week, while more than 80% of the economists polled anticipate a rate hike in December. Early signals from wage negotiations suggest that wage increases in 2027 could further reinforce inflationary stickiness. Consequently, a pause in rate hikes and an upward revision of the inflation outlook can coexist: the former reflects the pace of tightening, while the latter determines the direction of monetary policy.
This shift has also moved the market's focus from "whether there will be a rate hike this week" to where the terminal rate will ultimately settle. The Bank of Japan estimates the neutral rate to be in the range of 1.1%–2.5%, while institutions such as JPMorgan Securities and BNP Paribas project that the terminal rate for this cycle could reach 2.5%, higher than the market's current pricing of around 2%. articles.title: The Bank of Japan's "hawkish pause" is in place! With core inflation meeting the target, the path is paved for a return to rate hikes in December, while the yen regains its safe-haven appeal amid the AI-driven sell-off. - Moomoo
articles.summary: The Bank of Japan's "hawkish pause" is in place! With core inflation meeting the target, the path is paved for a return to rate hikes in December, while the yen regains its safe-haven appeal amid the AI-driven sell-off.  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
The Bank of Japan kept interest rates unchanged, stating that inflation has, for the first time, reached its target. While maintaining its benchmark rate, the central bank also indicated for the first time that underlying inflation has hit the 2% goal, a milestone that could pave the way for another rate hike as early as December.
Zhitong Finance APP learned that, as the market had anticipated, the Bank of Japan kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged during Friday's Asian midday session, following the monetary policy moves of the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. At the same time, in its official monetary policy statement, the Bank of Japan for the first time indicated that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target. This milestone can be seen as opening the door to a possible return to rate hikes as early as December and to the normalization of the future path of policy rates.
According to a statement from the Bank of Japan, the central bank kept its policy rate at 1.25% at the conclusion of its two-day meeting on Friday. All economists surveyed by major financial institutions had previously forecast this unchanged rate.
Achieving the inflation target means that the Bank of Japan must now shift from boosting inflation to ensuring it does not exceed the target level. The bank stated that keeping inflation near its current level going forward is "crucial," while warning that underlying inflation faces the risk of deviating upward from the target. Given these upside risks to inflation, more than 80% of surveyed economists expect the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates again in December.
As shown in the chart above, most seasoned observers of the Bank of Japan currently expect the central bank to raise interest rates again in December.
Junya Takemoto, a senior economist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, said: "At today afternoon's press conference, given how strongly the market is already anticipating a December rate hike, I'll be watching to see whether the Bank of Japan will reinforce those expectations or adopt a neutral stance. In the past, Governor Ueda has stated at press conferences that the Bank would closely assess developments ahead of its next meeting."
The Bank of Japan also announced that, starting in January, it will nearly triple the pace at which it sells exchange-traded funds it holds, with annual sales expected to total approximately 860 billion yen, or about 5.5 billion U.S. dollars. The bank stated that completing this process will take roughly 43 years, compared with more than 110 years at the previous sales rate.
The yen strengthened from 157.52 per U.S. dollar before the resolution was announced to around 157.12 per U.S. dollar.
Market attention has now shifted to the press conference scheduled for around 3:30 p.m. local time, to be delivered by Governor Kazuo Ueda. Investors will be closely scrutinizing the remarks for guidance on the next rate hike and any clues as to how high interest rates will ultimately climb during this tightening cycle.
The Bank of Japan was the last of the three major central banks to announce its decision this week, with both the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank also holding their policy rates steady. Last month, the three central banks raised interest rates in a coordinated move for the first time.
For the Bank of Japan, raising interest rates at two consecutive meetings would be an unprecedented move this century, potentially sending shockwaves through the markets. Japan's benchmark interest rate is already at a 31-year high, though it remains relatively low compared with other members of the Group of Seven.
The Bank of Japan's monetary policy statement indicated that the rate decision was approved by a vote of 8 to 1, with Takada Venture casting the dissenting vote in favor of a rate hike. Following its June rate increase, the Bank of Japan raised borrowing costs again on September 18, marking the shortest interval between rate hikes since 1990.
Following the Bank of Japan's decision to hold interest rates steady, the yen quickly extended its gains against the U.S. dollar. After the central bank kept rates unchanged as expected and, for the first time, signaled that underlying inflation has reached 2%, the yen's appreciation against the dollar widened.
Following the Bank of Japan's Monetary Policy Committee vote of 8 to 1 to keep interest rates unchanged, the yen briefly strengthened by 0.4% to 157.12 per U.S. dollar. All 53 Japanese economists surveyed by Bloomberg had previously anticipated this decision.
This trend unfolded on Friday as global markets shifted toward safe-haven assets, with tech stocks falling and oil prices rising. The yen has begun to signal a return to its traditional role as a safe haven. For years, during periods of market stress, the wider interest-rate differential and Japan's substantial overseas investment flows had exerted a stronger influence on the currency than safe-haven demand.
As shown in the chart above, following the Bank of Japan's policy decision, the yen-dollar exchange rate quickly widened its gains, underscoring the pace of the yen's appreciation.
OCBC Bank's FX strategist, Moh Siong Sim, said that the central bank's confirmation that its official inflation target has been met "signals further policy tightening ahead" and "should provide support for the yen." However, "the risk of another escalation in U.S.-Iran tensions following the U.S. midterm elections has pushed oil prices higher, potentially preventing the yen from fully benefiting from the weaker dollar environment driven by AI-related concerns."
Goldman Sachs strategists previously stated that, as Japan's policy environment shifts and global yields rise, the risk of a sharp yen depreciation has diminished, making the yen a more effective hedge against market shocks triggered by AI.
Last week, a selloff in global tech stocks boosted demand for safe-haven assets, pushing the yen to a more than one-month high of 156.08 per U.S. dollar.
Meanwhile, long-term Japanese government bonds have been performing strongly recently, with signs of a rebound in domestic demand and a more favorable policy environment further boosting the appeal of their higher yields. The yield on 30-year JGBs has already fallen by roughly 40 basis points from this month's peak of 4.25%.
The Bank of Japan announced that, starting in January, it will increase the annual pace of ETF sales from roughly 330 billion yen to about 860 billion yen. Following this announcement, Nikkei index futures on the Osaka exchange widened their losses. Meanwhile, Japanese stocks came under pressure alongside other global markets, as concerns over AI‑related spending and valuations sparked a sell-off in technology shares.
Shogo Karitani, a strategist at a Hong Kong bank, said: "The ETF‑selling plan came as a surprise. It is being viewed as a strong hawkish move by the Bank of Japan, as it signals further progress in monetary policy normalization, thereby prompting some modest yen buying."
As the scale of AI‑related infrastructure development among global technology firms continues to surge, driving overall corporate growth to record highs this year, yield metrics in the global credit bond market have steadily deteriorated. Consequently, financing costs for Japanese companies—particularly those tied to AI—have risen markedly, and credit spreads across various segments have widened broadly.
Traders will be watching the press conference by Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda following the decision, which typically begins at 3:30 p.m. Tokyo time.
The Real Shift Behind the "Hawkish Pause": Official Inflation Assessments Have Crossed a Key Threshold, and ETF Liquidations Have Accelerated Unexpectedly
The central shift in the Bank of Japan's latest decision is that interest-rate maintenance and the push to normalize policy will now proceed in tandem. On October 30, the bank voted 8–1 to keep its policy rate at 1.25%, in line with the expectations of all 53 economists surveyed by Bloomberg; only Takeshi Takada had advocated a 25-basis-point hike to 1.5%. The rate decision itself was no surprise, but the incremental information that most influenced market pricing was the bank's first confirmation that underlying inflation has broadly aligned with its 2% target, along with an announcement to accelerate the sale of equity ETFs. Following the release of the decision, the yen briefly widened its gains against the dollar to around 0.4%, reaching 157.12, while Nikkei futures extended their losses.
"Meeting the core inflation target" signals a shift in the Bank of Japan's assessment of the underlying price trend. The mutual reinforcement between wages and prices, coupled with stable medium- to long-term inflation expectations, has further tilted policy toward preventing an overshoot of inflation. In its official outlook, the bank revised up its forecast for the CPI excluding fresh food to 2.6% for fiscal year 2027, from 2.4%, while lowering its projection for real GDP growth over the same period to 0.7% from 0.8%, painting a picture of moderate growth amid still‑strong price pressures. The central bank has explicitly signaled its readiness to continue raising interest rates in response to economic, price, and financial conditions, making December the next key window of focus for markets; more than 80% of surveyed economists expect a rate hike at that meeting, though this does not constitute a formal commitment by the bank to any specific decision.
The acceleration of ETF sell‑offs has reinforced the signal that unconventional monetary easing is being unwound. Official documents indicate that, starting in January 2027, the annual sales volume—measured at book value—will increase from roughly JPY 330 billion to JPY 860 billion, about 2.61 times the previous level, corresponding to an estimated market value of approximately JPY 2.46 trillion. articles.title: Fed Pauses Interest Rate Hikes for Now as Key Midterm Election Looms - Realtor.com
articles.summary: Fed Pauses Interest Rate Hikes for Now as Key Midterm Election Looms  Realtor.com
articles.full_text:
Federal Reserve policymakers have put interest rate hikes on pause for now, as they wait to assess further data on inflation and the strength of the economy.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh joined the 10-2 majority on the Federal Open Market Committee on Wednesday, voting to leave the federal funds rate unchanged at its current range of 3.75% to 4.00%.
“Inflation remains elevated,” the committee's statement said. “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2% goal."
Dissenting were Fed Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, who both voted in favor of a quarter-point increase to the overnight rate. Hammack is known for her "hawkish" position on inflation and previously dissented in favor of higher interest rates. Cook, who is the target of removal efforts by President Donald Trump, has never dissented from the majority before.
At a press conference following the vote, Warsh also revealed that the FOMC will reduce its schedule of interest rate votes to seven next year and six in 2028, down from the current annual pace of eight votes.
Last month, the FOMC voted to raise rates for the first time in three years in an effort to clamp down on inflation. But now, with the crucial midterm elections less than a week away, a pause allows the Fed to avoid making political waves as voters head to the polls.
Warsh insisted the election had no bearing on the interest rate decision.
"I didn’t hear a reference to politics, elections, what’s happening in the next week or so,” Warsh said of the two-day FOMC meeting. “I don’t believe it had any role in the decision, not just for me, but my colleagues around the room.”
More rate hikes appear to be on the horizon. Investors now expect the Fed to raise rates by a quarter-point in December and at least once again in the first quarter of 2027.
Mortgage rates, which briefly dipped below 6% in late February, have marched steadily higher this year, fueled by the same inflation concerns that prompted the Fed to take action. Last week, mortgage rates averaged 7.32%, according to Freddie Mac.
The Fed uses higher interest rates to fight inflation and lower rates to stimulate the job market, in line with the central bank's dual mandate of maintaining price stability and maximum employment. The Fed doesn't directly set mortgage rates, which instead move in response to the bond market.
Bankrate housing market analyst Jeff Ostrowski says that mortgage rate gyrations since the last Fed policy meeting underscore the fact that the central bank doesn't control mortgage rates.
"The Fed raised its benchmark rate a quarter-point, and mortgage rates jumped three-quarters of a point in a month. The lesson? Mortgage rates move with 10-year Treasury yields, not the federal funds rate,” he says.
In recent months, bond investors have reacted with alarm over inflation, fueled by rising global oil prices amid the war with Iran. That sent the key 10-year Treasury yield higher, although bond markets have stabilized in recent weeks, bringing mortgage rates down slightly from a three-year high of 7.40%.
"Mortgage rates have not dropped back to their mid-September level, and the housing market is feeling the effects," says Realtor.com® Chief Economist Danielle Hale.
However, the economist notes home shoppers can still set themselves up for a better mortgage rate by boosting their credit, making a higher down payment, and shopping around for a mortgage.
"Those hoping to make a home purchase in the months ahead should plan for further mortgage rate volatility and rate-proof their home shopping budget by testing out a range of possible mortgage rates so they’ll be prepared to react," says Hale.
One expected dissent, and a surprising one
Of the 12 voting members of the FOMC, two dissented from the majority consensus: Hammack and Cook.
Hammack is widely viewed as the leader of the panel's hawkish faction and has not shied away from speaking out about the threat she believes persistent inflation poses to U.S. consumers and businesses.
The Cleveland Fed president, whose current term as a voting member started in January, previously dissented in favor of higher rates, voting against the majority in April and July of this year.
Cook, however, has never dissented from the majority decision since joining the Fed's Board of Governors in 2022. Dissents are typically more rare from Fed governors than from regional Fed presidents, who are usually more comfortable breaking ranks from the chairman.
Appointed by President Joe Biden to a 14-year term that expires in 2038, Cook has been at the center of a prolonged removal campaign by Trump.
Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, told CNBC that Cook's vote to raise rates may have been intended to send a message to Trump.
"This could have been a protest vote as the Trump administration is taking steps to get Fed Gov. Cook to resign one way or another," he said.
Trump, who vocally favors lower interest rates, attempted to fire Cook last year over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud in connection to the purchase of personal residences before joining the board.
No criminal charges have been brought in the matter, and the Supreme Court blocked Trump's attempt to remove Cook. Earlier this month, Trump renewed his push by directing a special committee to investigate the allegations against Cook.
What the Fed rate decision means for homebuyers
With inflation still running above the Fed's 2% target, prospective homebuyers shouldn't hold out much hope for instant relief on mortgage rates. A recent forecast from economists at the Mortgage Bankers Association projected that mortgage rates would remain above 7% through 2027.
Peter Zaitzeff, a top-selling agent with Serhant in New York City, says that "buyers should accept that 7%-plus rates are the new norm.
"Navigating high interest rates coupled with inflation and high consumer pricing is the new reality," he tells Realtor.com. "Buyers are more selective and are negotiating harder. We're seeing greater attention to monthly carrying costs and increased demand for sponsor concessions in new developments."
"Buyers need to adjust their expectations and recognize that higher mortgage rates may be here for the foreseeable future," adds Mendel Fellig, a real estate agent with Compass in Miami. "Historically, rates have been significantly higher, and buyers should focus on finding a property they love at a price they can comfortably afford rather than trying to time the market."
Indeed, the brief period in 2020 and 2021 when mortgage rates dipped below 3% marks the only time in modern history that mortgage rates have fallen that low.
Fellig says that in South Florida, limited inventory has kept many sellers confident in their pricing, while elevated borrowing costs have made buyers more cautious and price-sensitive.
"My advice to sellers is to remain flexible," he says. "If a property has been sitting on the market and a serious offer comes in, it's often better to bridge the pricing gap than hold out for an uncertain next offer. In today's market, realistic pricing and a willingness to negotiate are essential to getting deals done."
Jesse Ebner, a Colorado broker and owner of Ebner & Associates, says one potential upside of the higher-rate environment is less competition from other buyers.
"In certain situations, buyers may have more negotiating leverage, greater flexibility on terms, or opportunities to secure seller concessions," she says.
Ebner is already seeing the impact of higher interest rates on buyer behavior, negotiating dynamics, and the overall pace of the market.
"We’re seeing buyers become more deliberate and payment-conscious," she says. "They may take longer to make decisions, consider a smaller home, expand their geographic search, or become more selective about the features they’re willing to pay for. The monthly payment has become just as important as the purchase price, if not more."
Keith Griffith is a senior news editor at Realtor.com covering housing policy, real estate news, and trends in the residential market. Previously, his work has appeared in Business Insider, The Street, Chicago Sun-Times, New York Post, and Daily Mail, among other publications. He has a master's degree in economic and business journalism from Columbia University.

articles.title: USD/JPY Price Forecast — USD/JPY (157.86) Rises as the Yen Lags Ahead of the Fed and BoJ — 158.50 Target, 160 Intervention Cap - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: USD/JPY Price Forecast — USD/JPY (157.86) Rises as the Yen Lags Ahead of the Fed and BoJ — 158.50 Target, 160 Intervention Cap  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- USD/JPY rose 0.22% to 157.86 on Tuesday, recovering from Friday’s five-week low near 156 on AI stock selling.
- The U.S.-Japan two-year yield spread stood at 2.792 percentage points, keeping carry demand for dollars strong.
- The Bank of Japan is expected to hold at 1.25% on Friday, with a December hike to 1.50% the market’s base case.
USD/JPY traded at 157.86 in European hours on Tuesday, up 0.22% on the day, after opening at 157.50 and setting an early range of 157.41 to 157.77. The pair extended Monday’s 0.41% gain, when it rose from 156.81 to 157.45, and it now sits 1.9 yen above Friday’s five-week low near 156. The yen gave back half of last week’s rally in two sessions, and it underperformed every major currency on Tuesday: it lost 0.19% to the dollar, 0.37% to the New Zealand dollar, 0.19% to the Australian dollar, 0.15% to the Swiss franc and 0.13% to the Canadian dollar.
The broader picture shows a pair pinned near multi-decade highs. USD/JPY sits 3.7% above its level of 12 months ago and within a 52-week range of 151.54 to 164.00. It touched 158.95 on October 14 after a hot U.S. inflation reading and traded near 158.5 around October 20 on reports that the Bank of Japan was leaning against an October rate hike. Last Friday, a global selloff in technology and AI stocks sent haven flows into the yen and pushed USD/JPY down toward 156, its lowest in five weeks. Tuesday’s move reverses that haven rally as risk appetite returns.
The dollar side is firm. The U.S. Dollar Index traded at 102.20, near a two-week high, after durable goods orders rose 1.8% in September and consumer confidence jumped to 91.7. U.S. equities rallied, with the Nasdaq up 1.33% on AI optimism, a risk-on backdrop that typically weakens the yen as investors unwind safe-haven positions and return to carry trades.
The week holds two central bank decisions. The Federal Reserve announces at 2:00 p.m. ET Wednesday, with a hold at 3.75%-4.00% priced above 90% and a December hike close to fully priced. The Bank of Japan concludes its two-day meeting on Friday, October 30, with a hold at 1.25% expected and a December hike to 1.50% the market’s base case. Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference follows at 06:30 GMT Friday.
The yield gap remains the dominant force. The U.S.-Japan two-year yield spread stood at 2.792 percentage points on Monday, after narrowing 14.7 basis points. Investors earn nearly 2.8 percentage points a year to hold dollars over yen at the two-year tenor, a carry advantage that keeps steady demand for USD/JPY even as the BoJ tightens.
The thesis for this forecast is direct. USD/JPY is caught between carry and intervention. The rate differential favors the dollar and keeps buyers active on every dip toward 156. But Tokyo’s finance ministry has warned repeatedly that it stands ready to act, and the 160 level, where Japan intervened earlier this year, caps the upside. Both central banks are likely to hold this week, which leaves the pair in a 156 to 159 range until either the BoJ accelerates or Tokyo steps into the market.
How Tuesday’s Session Unfolded: Asia Bid, Europe Extends, Carry Resumes
The session followed the pattern of a market rebuilding carry positions after last week’s haven scare. USD/JPY opened in Asia at 157.50, near Monday’s close, and held a tight range through the Tokyo morning as Japanese markets digested data showing services producer prices rising 3.7%, a reading that supports the case for further BoJ tightening.
The Asian session saw little movement despite the hawkish data. Traders who expect a hold on Friday saw no reason to buy the yen on a single price index, and the pair traded between 157.41 and 157.67 into the European open. Japanese equities rallied with the Kospi and other regional markets on AI optimism after Anthropic’s IPO filing in the U.S., and risk-on sentiment in Asia weighs on the yen.
Europe extended the move. USD/JPY broke above 157.77, the Asian high, and climbed to 157.86 by 07:22 GMT, up 0.22%. The pair was trying to return above its 20-day exponential moving average on the daily chart, a level it lost during Friday’s haven rally. The dollar index firmed to 102.20, adding support.
The U.S. data added fuel. Durable goods orders rose 1.8% to $345.4 billion in September, and orders excluding transportation rose 0.5%. Consumer confidence jumped 7.5 points to 91.7, the highest since June and far above the 81.0 forecast. Strong U.S. data supports the Fed’s hawkish stance, which keeps the yield gap wide.
The cross-asset tone was risk-on. U.S. technology stocks rallied, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 3% and bitcoin held near $80,000. In that environment, the yen’s haven appeal fades and carry traders, who borrow in yen to buy higher-yielding assets, return to the market.
Tuesday’s move reversed most of Friday’s flight to safety. On Friday, the AI stock selloff drove investors into the yen, and USD/JPY dropped toward 156. Monday and Tuesday saw that haven demand unwind as equities recovered, taking the pair back toward 158.
For the forecast, the session confirms that the yen remains a funding currency in calm markets and a haven only in stress. Without a risk-off shock or a hawkish BoJ surprise, carry flows push USD/JPY higher toward the 158 to 158.50 resistance zone.
The Bank of Japan: A Hawkish Hold at 1.25% With December in Sight
The Bank of Japan is the force that should be strengthening the yen, and it is tightening at its fastest pace in decades. The BoJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September from 1.0%, in a 7-2 vote, three months after a hike in June. The September move took the rate to its highest level in 31 years and accelerated the hiking pace from roughly once every six months to once every three months.
Governor Ueda has shifted the bank’s focus. After nearly 14 years of trying to push inflation up to 2%, the BoJ now sees the risk running the other way. Speaking in Bangkok on October 16, Ueda said that with underlying inflation now close to 2%, the bank can no longer tolerate further increases and its main goal is to stabilize inflation around that level. At the October policy meeting, the BoJ is expected to declare victory over deflation and emphasize the risk that prices could overshoot.
This week’s decision is set up as a hawkish pause. The BoJ is expected to hold at 1.25% at the meeting ending Friday, October 30, by a majority vote. Ueda has said there is no need for back-to-back hikes, and that oversized or consecutive increases are reserved for situations where inflation rises rapidly beyond target. Market pricing gives a hold roughly 86% odds. Two board members, Takata and Tamura, may dissent in favor of a hike, which would signal the committee is leaning toward December.
December is the base case for the next move. Economists expect the BoJ to raise rates to 1.50% in December and maintain a quarterly pace. The policy rate at 1.25% now sits within the range of 1.1% to 2.5% that BoJ staff estimate as Japan’s neutral rate, the level that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. The bank is expected to stress that financial conditions remain loose, signaling room for further hikes before the rate reaches neutral.
Thursday’s data will shape expectations. Japan releases October CPI data and September unemployment before the decision, giving the BoJ a final read on inflation and labor conditions.
For USD/JPY, three outcomes matter. A hawkish hold with clear December guidance and two dissents would lift the yen modestly, pushing the pair toward 156.50. A hold with cautious language that lets hike expectations drift toward January would weaken the yen and send the pair toward 158.50. A surprise hike to 1.50%, priced near 14%, would trigger a yen rally toward 155.
The Fed on Wednesday: Hold at 3.75%-4.00%, December Hike Priced
The Federal Reserve decision lands two days before the BoJ, and it will set the dollar side of USD/JPY for the week. The FOMC began its two-day meeting Tuesday and announces its decision Wednesday at 2:00 p.m. ET, with Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference at 2:30 p.m. ET. Fed funds futures price a hold at 3.75%-4.00% above 90% probability, with a December hike to 4.00%-4.25% close to fully priced. Markets see no Fed rate cuts in 2026.
The Fed is still tightening. It raised rates in September as the U.S.-Iran war’s energy shock pushed CPI to 3.7% year over year and the Fed’s preferred PCE gauge to 3.4% in August. The October 14 CPI release, which beat forecasts, sent USD/JPY to 158.95, its high for the month, as traders priced a more aggressive Fed.
The U.S. data gives Warsh no reason to soften. Jobless claims fell to 194,000 in the week ended October 17, the lowest since late July. The U.S. flash composite PMI sits near a five-year high at 57.6, with selling prices rising at the sharpest rate since August 2022. Durable goods and consumer confidence beat forecasts Tuesday.
The two central banks are tightening in parallel, which keeps the yield gap wide. The Fed is at 3.75%-4.00%, the BoJ at 1.25%, a policy gap of 250 to 275 basis points. If both hike in December as priced, the Fed would move to 4.00%-4.25% and the BoJ to 1.50%, leaving the gap unchanged. That parallel tightening explains why the yen has not strengthened despite the BoJ’s fastest hiking pace in decades.
The three Fed outcomes matter for USD/JPY. A hold with neutral language that stresses data dependence and declines to commit to December would weaken the dollar and push the pair toward 156.50. A hold with explicit December guidance, the base case, would keep the dollar firm and support a test of 158.50. A surprise hike, priced below 10%, would send USD/JPY toward 159 to 160 and into Tokyo’s intervention zone.
The sequencing adds volatility. Wednesday’s Fed decision sets the dollar’s direction for Thursday’s Japanese data and Friday’s BoJ decision. A hawkish Fed followed by a cautious BoJ would be the most bullish combination for USD/JPY. A dovish Fed followed b

articles.title: Europe’s central bank chief, Christine Lagarde, steps down for ‘freedom of speech’
articles.summary: Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairsChristine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.Ending months of speculation about her future at the European Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president next February rather than October next year because ...
articles.full_text:
Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.
Ending months of speculation about her future at the European Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president next February rather than October next year because the rules of neutrality that governed her job prevented her from influencing debate about financial and economics affairs.
She spoke at the end of a press conference to explain the ECB’s decision to hold interest rates – maintaining its key deposit rate at 2.5% – despite inflation climbing to 3.8% last month, its highest since September 2023.
Lagarde said: “I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters.”
The former managing director of the International Monetary Fund has been tipped as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab, stepped down last year after being accused of financial and ethical misconduct, which he denies.
Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is struggling with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.
The European Council made up of EU heads of state appoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone.
There has been speculation that Lagarde, a former finance minister of France, has been encouraged to quit early by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, so her successor can be appointed before the possibility of a far-right or far-left presidential candidate being elected to the Élysée Palace. Lagarde will also be able to participate in next April’s elections.
She noted that ECB officials were bound by strict rules on not appearing partisan. “We have an obligation of neutrality; we comment on the situation with the focus on monetary policy,” Lagarde said, adding that the mandate was “the price we pay for being independent”.
Lagarde said she no longer felt comfortable staying silent on broader global issues. “I’m interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation,” she said, without elaborating.
Drawing on more than two decades in international economic and financial roles, she said she had more to contribute. “There are things that I can say – whether people will listen or not is another story. But I feel that I should say those things and I cannot do so in my current position.”
To reassure markets and staff that her early departure would not disrupt the central bank’s operations, she added: “A process has already started to identify my successor.” She said there were “plenty of excellent candidates.”
Macron said on Thursday that the succession at the ECB must be prepared in “an orderly and balanced way” with European partners, and also expressed his deep gratitude to Lagarde for her action during her tenure.
Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank, said: “The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027.
“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Élysée Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”
Lagarde joined the ECB in late 2019, shortly before the start of the Covid pandemic. During her tenure the central bank has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war, Donald Trump’s trade war and his war in the Middle East.
Lagarde was wearing two plasters on her face in her video message, which she said was because of “a small surgery earlier in the week”. She added: “Follow doctors’ orders and get your skin checked regularly.”

The dollar index DXY traded higher in the morning but fell after the FOMC outcome, ending the day -0.22% lower.
The FOMC left its federal funds rate target unchanged at 3.75-4.00% by a vote of 10-2, with two FOMC members (Cook and Hammack) dissenting and favoring a rate hike.
Join 200K+ Subscribers: Find out why the midday Barchart Brief newsletter is a must-read for thousands daily.
The market greeted the FOMC results as a bit dovish. Fed Chair Warsh reiterated the FOMC’s intent to bring inflation back to target, saying the FOMC has “made clear our readiness to act as circumstances require, and we have shown our willingness to act.”
However, some market participants apparently anticipate a more hands-off approach by the FOMC starting in 2027 as the Fed stretches out its rate-setting schedule. Fed Chair Warsh on Wednesday announced that one of the FOMC’s eight 2027 meetings will be non-voting and will focus on broad policy strategy, meaning there will be only seven voting meetings in 2027 versus eight in 2026. In 2028, two meetings will be non-voting broad-strategy meetings, reducing rate-setting meetings to six.
The FOMC results could also be seen as a bit dovish because Warsh said financial conditions have tightened, with borrowing becoming more difficult, suggesting the Fed may face less pressure to raise interest rates.
Still, markets are pricing in an 85% chance of a rate cut at the FOMC’s next meeting on December 8-9, little changed from before the FOMC results.
The dollar has underlying safe-haven support from Middle East tensions as concerns continue about Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and speculation about whether the US will launch a new military attack on Iran after Tuesday’s (Nov 3) US election. The Wall Street Journal reported late Tuesday that the US has told several Persian Gulf countries to be prepared for a short, intense military campaign against Iran. WSJ said President Trump hasn’t yet decided to proceed with the attack but is leaning toward an attack after next Tuesday’s mid-term elections.
Axios reported Wednesday that a US military operation is expected to include a week of massive strikes on Iranian leadership, energy, nuclear, and infrastructure targets, according to US and Israeli officials, if negotiations do not bear fruit. Axios reported that Qatar is leading behind-the-scenes mediation efforts, supported by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Türkiye.
In a bearish factor for the dollar, the Sep US trade deficit of -$134.9 billion was wider than market expectations of -$130.2 billion. Sep exports rose +2.4% m/m, weaker than expectations of +2.6%. Sep imports rose +2.6% m/m, stronger than market expectations of +1.3%.
EUR/USD M rose +0.02%. The yen has weakened this week, after last week’s safe-haven strength during the sharp sell-off in global stock markets.
The yen has underlying support on expectations that the BOJ will maintain a hawkish policy bias at its meeting this Friday, likely raising its inflation forecast for fiscal 2027. The odds of a BOJ rate hike at Friday’s meeting are very low at 1%, although those odds rise to 57% for a BOJ rate hike at the following meeting on December 18.
December COMEX gold (GCZ26) closed down -23.0 (-0.56%) on Wednesday, and December COMEX silver (SIZ26) closed down -0.847 (-1.55%).
Precious metals prices were undercut by the higher dollar seen during the morning, along with the +3 bp rise in the 10-year T-note yield.
Gold has underlying safe-haven support from Middle East tensions, with persistent attacks by the Houthis on Saudi targets and speculation about a possible new US military attack on Iran after next Tuesday’s US election.
Gold prices were undercut last Tuesday when Russia’s central bank reported reducing its gold reserves to 72.8 million ounces as of October 1, the lowest level in 7 years. Russia’s central bank is the sixth largest holder of gold among the world’s central banks.
Recent fund support for precious metals is bullish for prices, as long holdings in gold ETFs climbed to a 4.25-year high last Wednesday, although those holdings have since backed off. Long holdings in silver ETFs rose to a 7.5-month high on Monday.
Strong central bank demand for gold is supporting gold prices, after recent news showed that bullion held in China's PBOC reserves rose by 740,000 ounces to 77.47 million troy ounces in September, the largest increase in three years and the twenty-third consecutive month the PBOC boosted its gold reserves.

articles.title: Hedge fund leverage raises emerging market risks as global capital flows reverse - Hedgeweek
articles.summary: Hedge fund leverage raises emerging market risks as global capital flows reverse  Hedgeweek
articles.full_text:
Rising hedge fund leverage and crowded investment positions could amplify financial instability across emerging markets, as weakening global risk appetite and renewed monetary tightening trigger capital outflows, according to analysis by Research Fellow Iván Weigandi.
Emerging markets have demonstrated resilience throughout much of 2026 despite higher global interest rates and energy price volatility, supported by strong equity valuations and investor optimism surrounding artificial intelligence. Foreign investors allocated $246bn to emerging market bonds between January and September, partially offset by $114bn in equity outflows, while emerging market currencies appreciated 4.2% against the US dollar.
However, sentiment deteriorated sharply in September as expectations of further US monetary tightening pushed Treasury yields higher. Non-resident portfolio flows reversed from $11.4bn of inflows in August to $26.3bn of outflows in September, while emerging market currencies weakened 3% against the dollar. Sovereign, corporate and high-yield credit spreads widened by 35, 41 and 85 basis points respectively from 10 September.
The analysis identifies growing leverage among hedge funds and other non-bank financial institutions as a potential source of market disruption. Highly leveraged portfolios and concentrated positions could accelerate selling during periods of volatility, with margin calls forcing investors to liquidate emerging market assets and intensifying pressure on currencies and bond markets.
An AI-related market correction presents another significant risk, particularly for technology-exposed economies including South Korea, Taiwan, Malaysia and Vietnam. Further oil price shocks could also weaken emerging market financing conditions, especially among net energy importers already facing higher import costs and foreign currency pressures.
The report warns that the combination of leveraged investment strategies, interconnected financial markets and deteriorating global risk appetite could leave emerging economies exposed to further capital flight, despite improvements in domestic economic fundamentals.

articles.title: Fed Meeting Live Updates: Interest Rates Hold Steady Despite 'Elevated' Inflation - The New York Times
articles.summary: Fed Meeting Live Updates: Interest Rates Hold Steady Despite 'Elevated' Inflation  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
Latest
- The Federal Reserve held rates steady on Wednesday as expected. The two dissenting officials in favor of a quarter-point increase included Lisa D. Cook, a governor who is fighting to keep her job amid President Trump’s campaign to fire her. Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed’s chairman, leaned into the idea that the central bank had the flexibility to accumulate more information to make the right determination about rates because expectations about future inflation do not point to a lack of confidence in the Fed’s ability to eventually achieve the 2 percent target and because there are no signs the economy is overheating.
- Mr. Warsh’s biggest announcement of the day pertained to how often the Fed will vote on interest rates in the coming years, an idea that The New York Times first reported the chairman raised in July. In 2027, the Fed plans to hold seven policy meetings, with one dedicated to discussing “broad monetary policy strategy.” In 2028, there will be six policy meetings and two on strategy.
- Mr. Warsh repeatedly mentioned a shift in financial conditions since September, which he suggested helped the Fed in the pursuit of its inflation goal on the margins. Credit conditions have “tightened for some businesses and households, much as we would expect,” he said. “Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations, and while overall financial conditions are tighter, I’m unwilling and unable to call them tight. But broadly, these developments go in the direction of achieving a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.”
- The Fed’s meeting is days before the midterm elections, but Mr. Warsh emphasized that politics played no role in Wednesday’s decision to hold rates steady. But the political backdrop has been hard to ignore, especially because of Mr. Trump’s repeated attacks on the Fed for not complying with his demands for lower rates. The White House has demanded that Ms. Cook attend an in-person hearing to defend herself against allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, something Mr. Trump has cited as a reason to fire her.
The S&P 500 ended the day 0.3 percent higher, after a volatile period of trading while Warsh was speaking. Easier monetary policy, with rates expectations falling, is usually bullish for the stock market.
Starting next year, the Federal Reserve will reduce the number of meetings at which it sets interest rates, Kevin M. Warsh, the central bank’s chairman, announced Wednesday.
The Fed’s 12-member policy committee currently holds eight regularly scheduled meetings a year, a cadence it has maintained since the 1980s. Mr. Warsh, who took over as the Fed’s leader in May, raised the idea of reducing the number of meetings at the committee’s closed-door session in July, a discussion first reported by The New York Times and later confirmed in the publicly released minutes of the meeting.
In a news conference on Wednesday, Mr. Warsh said the Fed would meet eight times next year as usual. But only seven of those meetings will include a vote on interest rates. The eighth “will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy,” he said.
In 2028, the Fed expects to hold just six rate-setting meetings, with two meetings dedicated to discussions of longer-run strategy, Mr. Warsh said.
“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information rich intervals,” Mr. Warsh said, “but it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons.”
Some economists have criticized the idea of holding fewer meetings, arguing it could make it harder for the Fed to respond quickly to changes in inflation and the labor market. The move also fits a pattern during the early months of Mr. Warsh’s chairmanship toward providing less information to investors and the public, reversing a decades-long trend toward greater openness.
Other economists, however, have defended the idea. They argue that providing more time between meetings will make it easier for policymakers to identify meaningful shifts in economic conditions. And they note that the Fed can hold emergency meetings if necessary, as it has done numerous times in the past.
Investor expectations for interest rate increases have also fallen, further pointing to doubt about the Fed’s resolve to keep raising rates. Robert Dishner, a senior portfolio manager at Neuberger, said that while a December rate increase remains on the table, “the 2027 hikes that the market has priced in may require further consideration.”
There is an interesting dynamic in the market as investors digest Warsh’s comments. The short-dated, two-year Treasury yield has fallen to 4.71 percent, while the 10-year Treasury yield has risen to 5.04 percent. The move in the 10-year was driven by a rise in the breakeven inflation rate, which is a market measure of investors’ inflation expectations. “That to me is literally the market saying that you talk tough on inflation but you are not delivering on it,” said George Goncalves, head of U.S. macro strategy at MUFG Securities.
The biggest question coming into the news conference was why the Fed didn’t raise rates given the persistence of inflation. I’m not sure we ever got an answer, despite the best efforts of reporters to pin Warsh down.
Warsh says the economy is strong, but not necessarily too hot in a way that is leading to inflation. “Is the economy running too hot? Is the economy too strong? That isn’t the judgment of most of my colleagues,” he says. He argues that productivity growth is picking up, which allows the economy to grow faster without causing inflation.
Warsh reiterated his comments that he “does not believe” in forward guidance. However, he was careful to include a caveat for when the economy is in crisis. Recalling his experience during the 2008 financial crisis, he said that in those moments, guidance is needed.
Warsh is asked about the role that the A.I. investment boom is playing in driving both inflation and economic growth. He says that A.I. is an important factor in the strong economy, but not the only one. And he pushes back against the idea that A.I. investments are insensitive to interest rates, noting that corporate bond investors appear to be distinguishing between A.I. companies that they view as safe and those that could be riskier. In other words, he still believes interest rates will do the job of bringing inflation under control.
Warsh says that while surveys show that consumers are expecting faster inflation in the near-term, there is relatively little evidence that they are expecting faster inflation over the longer run. That’s generally true, but there have been some hints that consumers are expecting inflation to be higher in the future as well. Economists and policymakers pay close attention to such measures of expectations because if consumers and businesses start to expect inflation to endure, it can make it harder for the Fed to bring it under control.
Warsh is asked about the task forces that he convened to look at a wide range of issues that he believes are central to how the Fed conducts policy. They include groups looking at how the Fed communicates as well as how it models inflation. He said “some, but not all” groups will have recommendations by year-end, the deadline that Warsh initially set.
Reducing the number of meetings is the most major change that Warsh so far has announced at the central bank. The reason that Warsh most often cites is that it will allow for more data to accumulate between votes on interest rates. One potential risk is that it might leave the Fed less nimble to act if the economic backdrop rapidly changes. The Fed can hold emergency meetings, but they only tend to do that during periods of crisis.
Yields have come back down to 5 percent where they started the day. It appeared investors were responding to Warsh’s comments on inflation expectations remaining anchored, despite hotter inflation data in recent weeks. It’s obviously hard to know the precise driver but what is clear is that markets are twitchy, moving quickly higher and lower since Warsh started speaking.
Warsh says the committee is “going to be able to figure out what’s the appropriate protocol” and that he is “encouraged by the progress we’ve made in a short period of time.”
It isn’t clear what progress the Fed has made, given the hot September inflation readings. But he highlights the continued stability of inflation expectations, which he said indicates confidence that the Fed will do what is needed to bring inflation under control.
Colby leads off with the central question of the day: If inflation is so high, why not raise rates today? Warsh stresses that the Fed is committed to bringing inflation down to its 2 percent target and is willing to act to get there. But he doesn’t directly address why policymakers didn’t act today. “If the crux of your question is you haven’t achieved price stability, you’re right,” he says. But he says they are committed to getting there.
Bottom line: The Fed plans to hold only seven votes on interest rates next year, and six in 2028, down from eight in recent years. Warsh first raised the possibility of reducing the number of policy meetings over the summer.
Warsh announces that the Fed will meet eight times next year, as it has in recent years. But in a change, one of those meetings will focus “exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy” and will not include a vote on interest rates. Starting in 2028, the Fed plans to dedicate two meetings to such broader strategy.
All of that strong growth rhetoric has helped push up equity prices again, with the S&P 500 rising 0.2 percent. Bond yields have also continued to push higher, with the 10-year Treasury yield rising to 5.04 percent.

articles.title: Fed leaves interest rates unchanged despite inflation in the US - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Fed leaves interest rates unchanged despite inflation in the US  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
The United States Federal Reserve is set to hold interest rates steady in its final monetary policy decision before the US midterm elections.
The central bank will maintain rates at 3.75-4 percent, following a 10-2 vote, in line with expectations.
CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, indicated that there was more than a 90 percent chance rates would remain unchanged.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the Fed said in its press release announcing the decision on Wednesday. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”
The Fed noted how inflation continues to rise.
It also added, “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.”
The most recent Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed the annual inflation rate increasing to 3.7 percent in September, up from 3.4 percent in August, with energy prices largely accounting for the monthly surge.
There were signs earlier this month that the central bank would maintain benchmark interest rates, with the Fed’s chair for supervision, Michelle Bowman, advocating a “wait and see” approach.
“I don’t feel any urgency for taking further action at this point,” she said at this month’s International Monetary Fund-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. “We really need to take some time and understand how things will evolve.”
The decision comes before Thursday’s release of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index report, which is used by the central bank to assess inflation and inform its decisions.
Today’s Fed announcement follows an interest-rate hike rise last month, amid surging inflation – the first increase by the central bank since July 2023. The move drew criticism from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pressed the Fed to cut rates since taking office. At the time, he wrote on Truth Social that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”
The Fed’s next monetary policy meeting is scheduled for December 8-9, when it will give its final rate decision of the year.
Current forecasts point to a quarter-point interest rate increase.

articles.title: US Fed holds interest rates steady as inflation runs hot - www.thenationalnews.com
articles.summary: US Fed holds interest rates steady as inflation runs hot  www.thenationalnews.com
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday in a 10-2 vote, as officials opted for patience amid lingering inflation concerns.
“The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 per cent goal. The committee will achieve price stability,” Fed chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters.
Fed governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack voted against the decision, preferring to raise rates by 25 basis points.
Wednesday’s decision was expected to be a short reprieve from raising short-term interest rates after the Fed lifted the target range to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent last month. 
The UAE Central Bank, which follows Fed decisions because of the dirham's peg to the dollar, also kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.9 per cent.
Investors still anticipate a quarter-point increase when Fed officials meet for the final time this year in December, according to CME Group data. Most officials indicated in September they would be in favour of another rate increase this year, although some have said in public remarks since that they are in no rush to do so.
"The two hawkish dissents, the wording of the policy statement and prior comments from officials all suggest the central bank will hike rates in December," Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a note.
Asked why rates were held steady, Mr Warsh said ensuring price stability is not about "some fixed individual date in the calendar" or "some isolated data point". He also said he has noticed financial and credit conditions have tightened since the Fed met last month.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury held steady at about 5 per cent after Mr Warsh's news conference. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite all saw minor gains to end the trading session in the green.
Ahmed Azzam, head of financial market research at Equiti Group, said his remarks were less hawkish than the post-meeting statement indicated, although his base case remains a quarter-point increase in December.
"But the bigger question is whether the Fed is overestimating the economy's ability to absorb inflationary pressures through productivity gains, potentially leaving it facing a more persistent inflation problem and a longer 'higher for longer' cycle in 2027," Mr Azzam said.
Partly contributing to the inflation outlook is the Iran war's effect on energy prices. The Fed typically looks through energy costs because rate decisions cannot directly affect a loss of supply such as the one being experienced in the Middle East, although the prolonged conflict is testing this ability.
Petrol prices jumped 9.1 per cent in September on a monthly basis, representing more than half of the all-items monthly increase for the Consumer Price Index. For the past 12 months, petrol prices are up 34.2 per cent, while fuel oil is up 74.2 per cent. Overall, energy is up 20.4 per cent over the last year.
“Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy,” Mr Warsh said.
"I'm just telling you when I look out the window over the last several months, that is what we've seen. To the extent that oil prices were to move lower, again probably due to geopolitical events, that's something that we're going to have to interrogate.
"But that's just a hypothetical."
The labour market also appears to remain stuck. The economy added 29,000 jobs last month while the unemployment rate remained fixed at 4.2 per cent. This suggests economic activity is being fuelled by AI-driven investment instead of broad-based employment growth.
Fed officials have also acknowledged the artificial intelligence building as another inflation driver as Amazon, Meta and other so-called hyperscalers continue to spend billions on AI infrastructure. 
Mr Warsh said in Thailand earlier this month that central bankers have to recognise this AI investment as a “shock”, even as he sees it contributing to long-term wealth and productivity gains.
However, raising interest rates could have a muted impact on the hyperscalers, who are considered to be key drivers of the economy.
Morgan Stanley analysts said Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are expected to raise their total capital expenditure by more than 50 per cent in 2027, compared with 2026, and will probably be able to withstand higher funding costs.
Mr Warsh rejected that suggestion, saying he does not believe advanced technologies are “divorced from the rest of the economy".
Changes to meetings
Mr Warsh also laid out a new schedule for the regularly scheduled policy meetings. The Federal Reserve typically meets eight times a year to consider monetary policy decisions. 
Mr Warsh on Wednesday said it will keep the number of meetings unchanged for next year, although one meeting starting in autumn will exclusively focus on monetary policy strategy and not include a policy statement. He said this will grow to two meetings in 2028.
