articles.title: Fed holds rates steady despite concerns over inflation - CNBC
articles.summary: Fed holds rates steady despite concerns over inflation  CNBC
articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep benchmark interest rates on hold, opting to take a patient approach in its fight against inflation despite mounting evidence that price pressures are proving more nettlesome than policymakers had hoped.
In a widely expected decision, the Federal Open Market Committee kept the overnight funds rate in a range between 3.75%-4%, where it has been since the central bank approved a quarter percentage point increase in September.
"Inflation remains elevated," the post-meeting statement said. "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."
Two of the 12 FOMC voters dissented from the decision – Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, both of whom wanted the committee to raise rates by a quarter percentage point.
Cook has been at the center of a continuing controversy in which President Donald Trump has tried to remove her from office over allegations concerning information she provided on home loan applications. While the Supreme Court stopped the president's attempts, the administration has restarted the move, with a hearing scheduled for early November.
This was Cook's first dissent since joining the Fed in 2022 as an appointee of President Joe Biden.
Dallas President Lorie Logan and Minneapolis President Neel Kashkari both joined Hammack in voting no the last time the committee held, in July, and both have expressed the need for higher rates. However, they fell in with the majority Wednesday.
The midterm elections have lingered over the decision. Pivotal votes take place nationwide on Nov. 3, with control of Congress at stake. Fed officials consider political independence to be a cornerstone of the central bank, but some observers have speculated that officials won't want to raise rates this close to an election.
Trump, who nominated Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh to the position, has been at odds with the Fed for years. Trump has charged that the funds rate should be much lower.
The dissents reflected underlying conflict on the committee over how aggressively it needs to raise rates to combat rising prices. Inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, and the pace of price increases has only picked up since the September meeting.
Statements over the past several weeks, though, have reflected a desire to wait for additional data to come in before tightening policy further. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams both said current economic conditions allow policymakers time to evaluate their next move.
The statement characterized economic activity as "expanding at a strong pace," a seeming upgrade from "solid" in September. There were no other substantial changes to the statement other than the removal of a sentence that explained the September increase.
The decision came as little surprise as markets had been pricing in a less than 10% chance of a hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Following the decision, the S&P 500 held on to its gains.
However, it raises fresh questions about how long policymakers are willing to wait before tightening again. Futures market pricing indicates a strong possibility of another hike at the next FOMC meeting in December, and perhaps another increase or two in 2027.
Separately, Warsh unveiled at a news conference changes to the FOMC meetings next year that could reduce the number of rate-setting meetings each year.
"We believe eight meetings per year is the right number for the FOMC, but in 2027, one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," Warsh said. "The rest will be regular FOMC policy setting meetings, and I expect that in 2028 we'll have two meetings dedicated discussions of strategy and six for setting policy."
The Fed is up against a complicated economic and political picture. Inflation as measured by the Fed's preferred gauge is expected to be above 3% for September, even when excluding volatile food and energy prices. Economists are concerned that inflation has broadened beyond the energy sector and the impact from the Iran war.
At the same time, the unemployment rate has remained low and economic growth has been strong. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker is pointing to 3.4% annualized growth in the third quarter, which would be the strongest in a year. Consumer spending also has been solid, and investment tied to the artificial intelligence boom has helped keep the U.S. economic engine running.
The combination, though, has added to debate about how much restriction the Fed's current interest rate is actually exerting on the economy, and whether policymakers will need to move more aggressively if the price data doesn't improve.
While markets expect additional hikes, Warsh has avoided providing so-called forward guidance about the FOMC's intentions. In June, his fellow committee members, through the "dot plot" grid, indicated the likelihood of another increase this year.
"The Fed is taking a wait-and-see approach, and I think that makes sense given where we are in the cycle," said Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust and a former BLS analyst. "The economy is slowing, but slowing and breaking are two different things. Holding rates steady gives policymakers more time to assess how the economy is responding to September's hike and the recent rise in longer-term borrowing costs."

articles.title: 10-year Treasury yield creeps higher even as Fed keeps rates the same - CNBC
articles.summary: 10-year Treasury yield creeps higher even as Fed keeps rates the same  CNBC
articles.full_text:
Bond yields moved higher on Wednesday as investors digested the Federal Reserve’s decision to hold interest rates steady at its October meeting.
The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 3 basis points higher at 5.026%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, slipped more than 3 basis points to 4.704%.
The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — which tend to move on geopolitical events — was also up by more than 4 basis points to 5.354%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said the bank remained focused on “price stability” despite the pause and that the employment picture has been “quite positive.”
Despite the hold for October, expectations for a 25 basis points hike at the central bank’s next meeting on Dec. 9 currently stand at 85.7%, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.
More economic data is due Thursday. Personal consumption expenditures index — the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge — as well as the quarterly GDP growth rate and personal income and spending data will offer investors additional insights into the domestic economy and inflation picture.
That data will be critical to determining where the Fed may go from here, according to TruStage chief economist Steve Rick.
“Holding rates steady doesn’t necessarily mean the Fed is finished raising them, especially if inflation doesn’t start to cool,” he said. “Policymakers will want to see whether these price pressures are temporary or becoming more widespread throughout the economy.”
— CNBC’s Alex Harring contributed reporting.

articles.title: Euro-Dollar's Post-ECB Jump Flattered by USD Selloff - Pound Sterling Live
articles.summary: Euro-Dollar's Post-ECB Jump Flattered by USD Selloff  Pound Sterling Live
articles.full_text:
Image: Christine Lagarde. Felix Schmitt for ECB. Copyright (c) 2026 European Central Bank.
The euro rebounded against the dollar after softer U.S. inflation data and a tech-led retreat on Wall Street combined to overshadow the ECB decision.
EUR/USD rose from a fresh 2026 low just above 1.11 to 1.1163 on Thursday afternoon, with investment bank analysts tying the gains to a broad retreat in the dollar after the European Central Bank's decision.
The dollar is exposed to US Treasury yields, which fell after the release of US inflation data. "US rates slipped a few bps in the wake of the data, probably because of PCE deflators avoiding an upside surprise. Losses deepened in early US trading with an Alphabet-led tech sell-off prompting haven flows," says a note from KBC's markets desk.
The Pound to Dollar rate rose in step to 1.3367, a parallel move that marks the dollar as the driver. The euro lost ground against sterling over the same hours. EUR/GBP fell to 0.8356, equivalent to 1.1967 in GBP/EUR, after the Pound to Euro rate printed a fresh 17-month high at 1.1978 earlier in the day.
The dollar weakened even as US growth beat forecasts. The economy expanded at an annualised 3.4% in the third quarter, against a consensus of 3.2%, and core PCE inflation, the Federal Reserve's preferred measure, rose 0.3% in September for an annual rate of 3.1%.
The dollar lost support in the decimals of the inflation report, with economists at Barclays saying September's prices were "a touch softer than our translation". By Barclays' count, core PCE rose 0.32% on the month, 3bp below its forecast.
The dollar's exposure to the AI trade came via Alphabet where shares fell more than 10% after third-quarter results showed negative free cash flow of $9.07bn, against $2.70bn expected.
Above: EUR/USD pushes reacts to intial U.S. morning trade.
The dollar has leaned on AI investment for months; "burgeoning AI investment has previously proved largely a bullish US and USD story, via growth dynamics and investment inflows," says Jeremy Stretch, Chief International Strategist at CIBC.
The dollar's tech support was already in question ahead of the earnings round. Commonwealth Bank of Australia said in a recent update that "stronger-than-expected earnings and a more positive outlook, particularly for cloud revenue, would likely revive US tech optimism and could support the USD."
The Alphabet results open "another fissure in the AI trade just as it was gaining momentum," says Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.
Above: GBP/USD responds to the USD selloff.
ECB Keeps a December Hike Live
The euro drew little lift from the ECB, which held its deposit rate at 2.50% as President Christine Lagarde confirmed she will step down on 7 February 2027.
The euro weakened on the ECB's statement before Lagarde's press conference, with KBC citing the statement's new reference to tighter financing conditions. EUR/USD "recovered from the day's lows just above 1.11 to 1.115 during the press conference," says KBC.
The euro still has a December rate hike in its corner, "with today's comments, another rate hike at the ECB's December meeting is clearly in the offing," says Carsten Brzeski, Global Head of Macro at ING.
Above: Despite the ECB signalling a December hike, EUR/GBP is softer.
DNB Carnegie expects hikes to 2.75% in December and 3.00% in March. Deutsche Bank's Mark Wall sees December as "probably the end of the hiking cycle".
The euro gains less from that prospect because bond markets have already tightened conditions, "the key point for FX markets is that the ECB no longer needs to do all the tightening itself," says George Vessey, Lead FX and Macro Strategist at Convera.
The euro faces a leadership change that Holger Schmieding, Chief Economist at Berenberg, says "does not change the outlook for ECB policies". CIBC warns that the appointment of Klaas Knot, a known hawk, would bring "a hawkish repricing in the ECB rate strip".
What EUR/USD Needs to Sustain the Rebound
EUR/USD remains a sell on rallies for CIBC, which keeps "an immediate bias to fade EUR rallies" given growth concerns, high gas prices and elections in Spain and France.
EUR/USD would extend losses towards 1.1065, the May 2025 low, and then 1.0882 absent a close above the 16 October high at 1.1269, according to Stretch.
A EUR/USD "rebound... is likely to remain difficult to sustain, even if key support levels continue to hold," says Vessey.
The dollar keeps a hawkish Fed in reserve, with Barclays still expecting 25bp hikes in December and January. KBC says the Fed's outcome "might have been a different one" had it seen Thursday's data before Wednesday's meeting.
EUR/USD has a bullish counter-case in positioning, with the euro "deeply oversold" and able to "find its footing should the 'US exceptionalism' trade that has dominated in recent months begin to fade," says Karl Schamotta, Chief Market Strategist at Corpay.
EUR/USD needs a daily close above 1.1269 to turn the dollar's selloff into a recovery; until then, CIBC's 1.1065 target stays in play.

articles.title: Fed Holds Rates Despite High Inflation as Bank of England Faces Pressure Over Next Big Decision - International Business Times UK
articles.summary: Fed Holds Rates Despite High Inflation as Bank of England Faces Pressure Over Next Big Decision  International Business Times UK
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve has kept its key interest rate on hold at a 15‑year high of 3.75% to 4%, despite inflation running above target and public calls from President Donald Trump for lower borrowing costs.
The Bank of England now faces its own crucial choice on 5 November, as it comes under pressure over how to respond to price rises at home and shifting expectations in global markets.
The Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to maintain the target range. Two members favoured a quarter-point increase. The decision follows a rise in September that lifted the range to its current level and keeps US borrowing costs at their highest since before the financial crisis.
In its statement, the Fed said inflation remained elevated and that it needed more information before deciding on the appropriate policy stance. It reiterated its 2% inflation goal.
Further increases therefore remain possible, depending on incoming economic data and the outlook for growth and employment.
Officials signalled they were watching indicators such as wage growth, consumer spending and corporate investment for signs that higher rates are feeding through into slower demand. At the same time, they pointed to risks from global developments and financial conditions, which could tighten further even without another rate rise.
Warsh Insists Politics Played No Part
Asked whether political considerations had influenced the decision, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said politics had played no role in the committee's deliberations, according to Reuters.
Warsh said the Fed remained committed to returning inflation to its 2% target, while warning that higher energy prices could complicate that effort.
Trump has repeatedly called for lower interest rates. The Fed's decision comes days before the US midterm elections on 3 November, with inflation and the cost of living featuring in the political debate.
Analysts said the 10-2 split underlined that there is still a live debate within the Fed over how restrictive policy needs to be to return inflation to target. The two votes for a rise suggested that, if inflation stays firm or accelerates, further tightening is still on the table.
US Inflation Still Driven By Energy Costs
US consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months to September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The consumer price index rose 0.6% over the month, with energy prices up 5.2% and gasoline prices up 9.1%.
Economists noted that underlying price pressures in areas such as services, rents and wages would be crucial in determining the Fed's next steps. If energy-driven increases begin to feed into expectations and wage bargaining, policymakers could find it harder to bring inflation back to 2% without a more pronounced slowdown in activity.
What The Fed's Move Means For Britain
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee is due to announce its next decision on 5 November. It held Bank Rate at 3.75% in September.
UK inflation stands at 3.1%, above the Bank's 2% target. The Bank has said that disruption to energy supplies linked to the Middle East conflict has pushed up energy prices, and that these are expected to push inflation higher still.
The Fed's decisions do not determine the Bank of England's policy. However, changes in US interest rates can influence global bond yields and currency markets, which the Bank must assess alongside UK inflation, economic growth and labour-market data.
A high-for-longer Fed stance can put upward pressure on UK market rates, affecting government borrowing costs, corporate financing and, in time, mortgage and loan rates faced by households.
The MPC will weigh those external influences against domestic signs of cooling demand and the impact that previous increases in Bank Rate are already having on the housing market and business confidence.
Both central banks are trying to bring inflation back to target while avoiding unnecessary damage to economic activity. The Fed's decision to hold, with two members voting for an increase, shows that US policymakers are still weighing the possibility of further tightening, a debate that is also shaping the choices now confronting the Bank of England.

articles.title: Fed votes in split decision to hold interest rates steady despite sticky inflation - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Fed votes in split decision to hold interest rates steady despite sticky inflation  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
With the midterm elections less than a week away, the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, even as the latest inflation reports show prices rising again.
The central bank voted in a split decision to hold its benchmark interest rate steady in the range of 3.75% to 4%, after raising rates last month for the first time in more than three years.
Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack and Fed governor Lisa Cook broke ranks, preferring to raise rates by a quarter percentage point. This is the second time since July Hammack has dissented in favor of raising rates and Cook's first dissent in her tenure.
Read more: Follow live updates from the Fed's October meeting
Officials said they are focused on reviewing additional data to inform future rate decisions, adjusting their policy statement to say that "the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee's 2% goal."
The latest inflation reports show price growth has accelerated since September's hike.
The Consumer Price Index clocked in at 3.7% last month from 3.4% in August. Stripping out volatile food and energy prices — the way the Fed likes to scrutinize underlying inflation — CPI rose 2.6%, compared with 2.4% in August. Wholesale prices jumped more than 6% last month, and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the core Personal Consumption Expenditures Price index, due out Thursday — is projected to top 3%.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, in a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, acknowledged that the job of containing inflation is unfinished.
"If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine [is] starting to work some, but there's no firm conclusions," Warsh said. "I'm encouraged by the progress we've made in a short period of time. But if the crux of your question is 'you haven't delivered yet, you haven't achieved price stability,' you're right about that.
"But we're working on it."
Read more: What the Fed's interest rate decision means for your money
Warsh announced a change to the Federal Open Market Committee's meeting schedule, beginning next year. They will still meet eight times a year, but one meeting will "focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," Warsh said.
In 2028, he said, two meetings will be dedicated to strategy and six to setting policy.

articles.full_text:
Key Moments
- The People’s Bank of China set the USD/CNY central parity rate at 6.7147 for the upcoming Thursday session.
- The new fixing compared with the previous day’s reference rate of 6.7165.
- The latest central rate differed from the 6.6596 estimate reported by Reuters.
Updated USD/CNY Central Parity Rate
The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) set the USD/CNY central reference rate for the upcoming Thursday trading session at 6.7147. This compares with the prior day’s fixing level of 6.7165 and a Reuters estimate of 6.6596 for the latest setting.
| Parameter | Value | 
|---|---|
| Latest USD/CNY central rate (Thursday) | 6.7147 | 
| Previous day’s fix | 6.7165 | 
| Reuters estimate | 6.6596 | 
Mandate and Role of the People’s Bank of China
The People’s Bank of China is responsible for maintaining overall price stability, which includes managing exchange rate stability, while also supporting economic growth. In addition, the central bank seeks to advance financial sector reforms, including efforts to open and further develop China’s financial markets.
Ownership and Governance Structure
The PBOC is owned by the state of the People’s Republic of China, and as such is not regarded as an independent institution. Oversight and strategic direction are heavily shaped by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) Committee Secretary, who is nominated by the Chairman of the State Council. This role is more influential than that of the governor. Mr. Pan Gongsheng currently holds both the CCP Committee Secretary position and the governorship.
Policy Toolkit and Benchmark Rates
The PBOC employs a wide range of monetary policy instruments, which differs from the common frameworks used in many Western economies. Its key tools include the seven-day Reverse Repo Rate, the Medium-term Lending Facility, foreign exchange interventions, and adjustments to the Reserve Requirement Ratio.
China’s benchmark for lending costs is the Loan Prime Rate (LPR). Movements in the LPR directly affect the borrowing rates applied to loans and mortgages, as well as the returns on savings. By changing the LPR, the central bank can also impact the exchange rate of the Chinese renminbi.
Private Banking Presence in China
China permits privately owned banks to operate within its financial system, with 19 such institutions currently in existence. These entities represent a relatively small portion of the overall banking landscape. Among them, prominent digital lenders include WeBank and MYbank, which are supported by technology firms Tencent and Ant Group, according to The Straits Times.
In 2014, authorities allowed domestically owned banks that are fully funded by private capital to participate in the largely state-controlled financial sector.

articles.title: US Fed holds interest rates steady as inflation runs hot - The National
articles.summary: US Fed holds interest rates steady as inflation runs hot  The National
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday in a 10-2 vote, as officials opted for patience amid lingering inflation concerns.
“The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 per cent goal. The committee will achieve price stability,” Fed chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters.
Fed governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack voted against the decision, preferring to raise rates by 25 basis points.
Wednesday’s decision was expected to be a short reprieve from raising short-term interest rates after the Fed lifted the target range to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent last month. 
The UAE Central Bank, which follows Fed decisions because of the dirham's peg to the dollar, also kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.9 per cent.
Investors still anticipate a quarter-point increase when Fed officials meet for the final time this year in December, according to CME Group data. Most officials indicated in September they would be in favour of another rate increase this year, although some have said in public remarks since that they are in no rush to do so.
"The two hawkish dissents, the wording of the policy statement and prior comments from officials all suggest the central bank will hike rates in December," Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a note.
Asked why rates were held steady, Mr Warsh said ensuring price stability is not about "some fixed individual date in the calendar" or "some isolated data point". He also said he has noticed financial and credit conditions have tightened since the Fed met last month.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury held steady at about 5 per cent after Mr Warsh's news conference. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite all saw minor gains to end the trading session in the green.
Ahmed Azzam, head of financial market research at Equiti Group, said his remarks were less hawkish than the post-meeting statement indicated, although his base case remains a quarter-point increase in December.
"But the bigger question is whether the Fed is overestimating the economy's ability to absorb inflationary pressures through productivity gains, potentially leaving it facing a more persistent inflation problem and a longer 'higher for longer' cycle in 2027," Mr Azzam said.
Partly contributing to the inflation outlook is the Iran war's effect on energy prices. The Fed typically looks through energy costs because rate decisions cannot directly affect a loss of supply such as the one being experienced in the Middle East, although the prolonged conflict is testing this ability.
Petrol prices jumped 9.1 per cent in September on a monthly basis, representing more than half of the all-items monthly increase for the Consumer Price Index. For the past 12 months, petrol prices are up 34.2 per cent, while fuel oil is up 74.2 per cent. Overall, energy is up 20.4 per cent over the last year.
“Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy,” Mr Warsh said.
"I'm just telling you when I look out the window over the last several months, that is what we've seen. To the extent that oil prices were to move lower, again probably due to geopolitical events, that's something that we're going to have to interrogate.
"But that's just a hypothetical."
The labour market also appears to remain stuck. The economy added 29,000 jobs last month while the unemployment rate remained fixed at 4.2 per cent. This suggests economic activity is being fuelled by AI-driven investment instead of broad-based employment growth.
Fed officials have also acknowledged the artificial intelligence building as another inflation driver as Amazon, Meta and other so-called hyperscalers continue to spend billions on AI infrastructure. 
Mr Warsh said in Thailand earlier this month that central bankers have to recognise this AI investment as a “shock”, even as he sees it contributing to long-term wealth and productivity gains.
However, raising interest rates could have a muted impact on the hyperscalers, who are considered to be key drivers of the economy.
Morgan Stanley analysts said Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are expected to raise their total capital expenditure by more than 50 per cent in 2027, compared with 2026, and will probably be able to withstand higher funding costs.
Mr Warsh rejected that suggestion, saying he does not believe advanced technologies are “divorced from the rest of the economy".
Changes to meetings
Mr Warsh also laid out a new schedule for the regularly scheduled policy meetings. The Federal Reserve typically meets eight times a year to consider monetary policy decisions. 
Mr Warsh on Wednesday said it will keep the number of meetings unchanged for next year, although one meeting starting in autumn will exclusively focus on monetary policy strategy and not include a policy statement. He said this will grow to two meetings in 2028.

articles.title: Column: A hawkish Fed, shaky tech and the risk of an earnings letdown - TradingView
articles.summary: Column: A hawkish Fed, shaky tech and the risk of an earnings letdown  TradingView
articles.full_text:
Markets are now heading into the last two months of the year, having closed out October with a flurry of significant events.
First off, the US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, and Bank of Japan all held monetary policy meetings in the final week of October, and interest rates were left unchanged, as expected.
That removes a potential short-term headwind for equities.
Yet there’s still a general expectation that central banks will tighten monetary policy before the year-end, due to stubbornly high inflation.
Focusing on the US, the CME’s FedWatch Tool puts the probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike in early December at around 70%.
And if it once again chooses to leave rates on hold through to the year-end, then there’s less than a 10% chance that it won’t have hiked by mid-March 2027.
The interesting thing is that markets were more hawkish before the Fed meeting than after.
This is despite two FOMC members voting for an increase on Wednesday. Some observers considered that choice to be performative.
That could be the case, knowing that the majority wanted to hold, and given the problems that another hike would cause coming just a few days before the dreaded midterms – more in a minute.
But when it comes to pricing pressures, who can blame them? The major inflation updates released earlier this month were horrible.
September Core and Headline CPI both came in way above expectations and the prior month’s readings, with Headline being the highest number year-on-year since May.
Following this, the PPI data (the key measure of wholesale inflation, which typically leads consumer prices) proved to be even more shocking, with Core and Headline hitting highs last seen nearly four years ago.
To top it all, the day after the Fed left rates on hold, Core PCE, still the Fed’s preferred inflation measure and the one used for its 2% target, ticked up to 3.1% from 3.0%.
Not only is it moving in the wrong direction, but the last time it was below the Fed’s target rate was in February 2021.
Perhaps the Fed is hoping that a new virus will come and do its job for it again.
Failing that, if the tech sector selloff accelerates from here, the Fed could soon be cutting rather than hiking.
Bear in mind, the Fed, under its newish Chair Kevin Warsh, has made it clear that it will now be led by the data, rather than guiding the markets to a preordained route for monetary policy.
It has also said that getting inflation back down to its 2% target remains its number one priority.
Yet there was a dismal Non-Farm Payroll update in early October, along with an unwelcome uptick in the Unemployment Rate.
And it’s not the first time that payrolls have disappointed since the summer.
This has led some observers to wonder about the underlying health of the US economy once growth from the AI infrastructure buildout is subtracted.
That’s not to say that the AI trade isn’t genuine, only that it is highly concentrated and in danger of unravelling if certain optimistic assumptions don’t play out as currently priced.
And that brings us to the third quarter earnings season.
Earnings growth has been the biggest tailwind for US equity markets for years now.
And it is expected to continue into this quarter as well, with a year-on-year earnings growth rate forecast around 30%.
That could well come to pass. But results from Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon have really put the skids under the hyperscaler trade.
Meanwhile, and ahead of the upcoming Anthropic IPO, the only listed frontier lab, SpaceX, is trading at its lowest level in two months.
The chip sector looks like a bloodbath, and neoclouds aren’t looking particularly perky either.
Who knows how this will play out. Another ‘buy the dip’ opportunity?
Investors are now preparing for the midterm elections on the 3rd of November.
History shows that what happens after midterm elections has little overall effect on US stock market performance.
Corporate earnings, economic growth, employment, inflation and interest rates tend to matter far more.
Despite this, there have been times when politically sensitive sectors such as energy, healthcare and tech have faced different degrees of scrutiny following a change in control of Congress.
That can lead to a period of sector rotation, rather than the whole market moving one way.
Aside from this, a look at past midterms shows that political gridlock is a common outcome, and that often goes down well with financial markets.
The president’s party usually loses seats, and a split government is often seen as placing a limit on what an administration can do.
That could be considered a significant issue in the current political environment.
The polls close on the 3rd of November, and prediction markets suggest that a Republican-controlled Senate and a Democrat-controlled House are the most likely outcome.
This will be both an annoyance and a constraint for President Trump.
But it won’t affect his ability to issue executive orders, as well as deciding much of trade and foreign policy, including going to war.
So, as October draws to a close, the biggest challenge remains beating lofty earnings expectations. What could possibly go wrong?
(This is a fortnightly column by David Morrison. He is a Senior Market Analyst at Trade Nation. Views are his own.)

articles.title: Gold hits one-year low, silver slips below $50 as inflation fears bite - The Times of India
articles.summary: Gold hits one-year low, silver slips below $50 as inflation fears bite  The Times of IndiaSilver’s Sharp Correction: Is October Selloff Creating a Major Buying Opportunity?  Investing.com IndiaSilver Futures Drop to Rs 1.85 Lakh/kg on MCX  Rediff MoneyWizSilver slips below $50, hits 11-month low; should investors buy the dip?  Moneycontrol.comSilver tumbles Rs 8,300 to hit 11-month low at Rs 1.90 lakh per kg  ThePrint
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: Precious metals are having a rough run, with the latest sell-off taking gold to a one-year low and pushing silver below the $50-an-ounce mark for the first time since almost a year.
Rising energy prices and stubborn inflation concerns are weighing on investor sentiment, with expectations growing that US interest rates could stay higher for longer. Both metals extended their monthly losses on Friday, with silver taking a sharper hit.
Gold continued its downward journey on Friday, with spot prices falling 2.7% to $3,910.53 per ounce. This was the metal's lowest level since October 2025. US gold futures for December delivery also slipped 2.8% to $3,919.60 per ounce.
Bullion prices have declined 5.9% so far this month and are on track to record their second consecutive monthly fall.
Silver fared worse, with spot prices dropping 5.8% to $49.34 per ounce. The decline took the metal below the $50 mark for the first time since November 2025, bringing it to its lowest level since that month.
Why are precious metal prices falling?
The prospect of interest rates staying elevated for longer is putting pressure on precious metals. 
Higher energy prices have added to inflation concerns, prompting central banks to maintain a cautious stance on monetary policy.
Major central banks kept interest rates unchanged this week, but their indications suggested that the tightening cycle may not be over. The US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank both flagged inflation risks stemming from surging energy costs.
"Ongoing concerns about inflation have multiple central banks continuing to tilt hawkish," said Peter Grant, vice president and senior metals strategist at Zaner Metals.
"Even though holds were delivered by major central banks this week, the indication was that the higher-for-longer theme prevails, and that's weighing on precious metals."
US inflation data released on Thursday further strengthened these concerns. Inflation accelerated in September as consumers paid more for gasoline and other goods, bolstering economists' expectations of an interest rate hike in December.
Tech stock sell-off adds to precious metals pressure
The sharp decline in technology stocks may have added to the pressure on precious metals, with analysts at Commerzbank pointing to the possibility of forced selling and margin calls following the tech stock sell-off.
However, the analysts believe the fall in precious metal prices has been excessive and expect a recovery.
"We consider the fall in precious metal prices to be exaggerated and continue to expect a recovery," they added.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq was also poised for steep losses at Friday's opening as concerns over artificial intelligence spending weighed on technology stocks.
Meanwhile, oil prices continued to climb and were headed for a fourth consecutive monthly gain. Rising energy costs have strengthened expectations of interest rates remaining elevated for an extended period, making non-yielding assets such as gold less attractive.
Asian gold demand remains subdued
Weak physical demand in key Asian markets has added to the challenges facing gold.
Back at home, buyers held back from making purchases this week, expecting prices to decline further.
Meanwhile, demand in China, the top gold-consuming country, also remained muted, offering little support to the market.
The sell-off extended to other precious metals as well. Platinum prices dropped 4% to $1,428.35 per ounce, their lowest level since September 2025.
Palladium fell 3.1% to $975.25 per ounce, touching its lowest level since June 2025. Both metals were poised to register declines for the week as well as the month.

articles.title: Chart of the Day: USDJPY After Fed and BoJ decisions. Is Japan getting closer to another rate Hhike? - XTB.com
articles.summary: Chart of the Day: USDJPY After Fed and BoJ decisions. Is Japan getting closer to another rate Hhike?  XTB.com
articles.full_text:
USDJPY came under pressure following the conclusion of the Federal Reserve's and Bank of Japan's October meetings. Both central banks decided to leave interest rates unchanged, but differences in their communication point to diverging approaches to the next stages of monetary policy. The message from Tokyo was particularly significant, as policymakers sent a clearer signal that further monetary tightening remains on the table.
Source: XTB Research
Key factors currently shaping USDJPY
Bank of Japan holds rates but delivers a clearly hawkish message
The Bank of Japan left its key interest rate unchanged at 1.25%, in line with market expectations. However, the accompanying statement proved important for the future outlook of monetary policy. The BoJ indicated that underlying inflation in Japan is now broadly consistent with its 2% target. This marks a significant shift in the assessment of economic conditions, as achieving sustainable price stability was one of the main prerequisites for further monetary policy normalisation.
The central bank also raised its underlying inflation forecast for fiscal year 2027 from 2.4% to 2.6%, while indicating that the balance of risks to prices remains tilted to the upside. This suggests that policymakers see the possibility of inflationary pressures persisting at a higher level than previously anticipated.
The voting outcome is also worth noting. The decision to keep rates unchanged passed by an 8-1 majority. Board member Hajime Takata voted in favour of an immediate rate hike to 1.50%, arguing that with inflation close to target, the central bank should move more quickly towards a more neutral interest rate level. This disagreement highlights increasingly visible calls within the BoJ for a faster pace of monetary policy normalisation.
December BoJ rate hike becoming increasingly realistic
The October meeting strengthened expectations of another BoJ move before the end of the year. If the central bank decides to raise rates in December, the policy rate would increase from 1.25% to 1.50%. However, this outcome is far from guaranteed. Policymakers will need to assess the state of household consumption, labour market conditions and the impact of previous monetary tightening on economic activity.
Energy prices and their impact on inflation will also remain important factors. The BoJ will need to determine whether price pressures are sufficiently persistent to justify further rate increases. From the foreign exchange market's perspective, the key question is whether upcoming comments from central bank officials will reinforce December as a realistic date for the next rate adjustment.
Fed also holds rates, but inflation leaves little room for a dovish shift
The Federal Reserve decided to leave interest rates unchanged within the 3.75–4.00% range. However, the voting outcome revealed a lack of full agreement among FOMC members regarding the future direction of monetary policy. Two Fed officials, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, voted in favour of a 25-basis-point rate hike. This signalled that some policymakers consider the current level of interest rates insufficient to effectively contain inflationary pressures.
Meanwhile, Chair Kevin Warsh emphasised the need for more information before making further decisions. The Fed wants to assess how previous monetary tightening is affecting the economy, particularly amid elevated energy costs and rising investment expenditure related to the development of artificial intelligence.
PCE inflation accelerates again. The dollar retains an important source of support
Another factor complicating the USDJPY outlook is the latest US inflation data. September's PCE index, the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, increased by 0.5% month-on-month, compared with 0.3% in August. Annual inflation accelerated from 3.4% to 3.6%. Price pressures therefore remain persistent and significantly above the central bank's 2% target.
Under these conditions, the Fed has limited room to ease monetary policy. Persistently elevated inflation could even justify further monetary tightening. Following the October meeting, markets priced in a probability of a December rate hike exceeding 80%. This is an important argument against the assumption that the monetary policy gap between the two central banks will narrow rapidly.
USDJPY after central bank decisions: further correction or a return to gains?
The current situation points to an increasing risk of further yen appreciation, but does not confirm a lasting reversal in the broader USDJPY trend. In a bearish scenario, the key factor will be confirmation from the BoJ that it is prepared to raise interest rates in December. A further decline in US Treasury yields would provide additional support for the Japanese currency.
The opposite scenario assumes that the dollar remains strong due to persistent inflation in the United States, while expectations of another BoJ rate hike are pushed further into the future. In that case, the yen's current appreciation could prove to be merely a correction within a broader upward trend in the currency pair.
The risk of intervention by Japanese authorities should also remain on investors' radar. The 160 level remains an important reference point, although it is not an automatic threshold that would necessarily trigger action from Tokyo. The possibility of intervention may continue to limit the pair's upside potential, particularly in the event of a rapid depreciation of the yen.
Conclusion
The October meetings of the Fed and BoJ resulted in unchanged interest rates, but it was the Japanese central bank that delivered the more hawkish message. The upward revision of its underlying inflation forecast for the next fiscal year to 2.6%, together with the vote in favour of an immediate rate hike to 1.50%, increases the significance of the December meeting.
At the same time, persistent inflation in the United States and hawkish voices within the FOMC mean that the dollar continues to enjoy meaningful fundamental support. In the short term, the BoJ's more hawkish communication may favour the yen and limit USDJPY's upside potential. However, the pair's ultimate direction will depend on whether expectations surrounding the December decisions of both central banks are confirmed by incoming economic data.
Key factors for USDJPY:
- Hawkish BoJ: Rates remain at 1.25%, but the central bank signals that further monetary tightening remains possible.
- Japanese inflation: Underlying inflation is broadly consistent with the 2% target, while the FY2027 forecast has been raised to 2.6%.
- December rate hike: The possibility of the BoJ raising rates from 1.25% to 1.50% remains an important supportive factor for the yen.
- Fed and PCE inflation: Inflation accelerating to 3.6% year-on-year limits the scope for monetary policy easing.
- US Treasury yields: A decline in yields could put additional pressure on the dollar against the yen.
- Intervention risk: Japanese authorities may still respond to excessive weakness in the domestic currency, particularly near the 160 level.
- Base scenario: The BoJ's more hawkish stance increases the risk of a further downward correction in USDJPY, although persistent US inflation limits the yen's appreciation potential.

articles.title: The AI Tightrope: How the Artificial Intelligence Boom is Propelling Global Growth While Teetering on the Edge of Systemic Risk - Vocal
articles.summary: The AI Tightrope: How the Artificial Intelligence Boom is Propelling Global Growth While Teetering on the Edge of Systemic Risk  Vocal
articles.full_text:
At the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, top economic officials warn that a sudden faltering in AI investment could trigger a global market correction, urging a delicate balance between breakneck innovation and robust regulatory safeguards.
The artificial intelligence revolution has undeniably become the primary engine of global economic growth, cushioning the world economy against severe geopolitical shocks. However, at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings this week, a chorus of top policymakers and financial experts issued a stark warning: the global economy is becoming dangerously over-reliant on AI investment, and a sudden loss of momentum in the sector could trigger widespread financial instability.
The Undeniable Growth Catalyst
Propelled by massive capital expenditures on data centers, microchips, and related infrastructure, the AI boom has acted as a vital economic shock absorber. According to a new report released Tuesday by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), AI-related trade has significantly softened the global economic impact of soaring energy prices driven by the ongoing war in the Middle East.
The data underscores the technology's pervasive influence. Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s chief economist, highlighted that global trade surged by 8.3% between 2023 and 2025. Strikingly, she noted that without the explosive demand for AI-related products, that figure would have been a mere 4.6%.
“It is everywhere in the global economy,” Tenreyro observed. This sentiment was echoed by Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem, who emphasized the technology's deep integration into global finance. “You see it in GDP. You see it in the stock market. You see it in the bond market… So it is here, and it’s just the beginning,” Macklem stated.
The Looming Specter of an AI Bust
Despite the current euphoria, top officials in Bangkok cautioned against the systemic vulnerabilities inherent in a market so heavily concentrated around a single, unproven technological paradigm.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh described AI as the “most consequential change” to the global economy in his lifetime, acknowledging its “huge benefit.” However, he warned that the transition would be far from smooth. “The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one,” Warsh said, citing uncertainties surrounding both the fundamental understanding of the technology and the eventual market structure of these new industries.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva reinforced this caution, noting that because the AI boom is now so deeply woven into the fabric of global growth, any slowdown in the industry “would be felt across the world.” She warned that a loss of investor confidence could lead to capital flight from the sector, creating severe financial stability risks.
The IMF’s latest projections quantify this danger: a sustained decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4% by 2028. The report explicitly warned that “weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction,” echoing fears of a speculative bubble similar to the dot-com crash, but on a much larger, more interconnected scale.
Geopolitical and Regulatory Headwinds
Compounding the financial risks are severe geopolitical and regulatory headwinds. While AI trade has thus far helped offset the economic damage of the Middle East conflict, economists at Moody’s Analytics warn that a drawn-out war could ultimately “puncture” the AI boom. Prolonged conflict threatens to keep energy prices elevated and financial conditions tight, which would drive up operating costs and interest rates. This, in turn, could cast serious doubt on the long-term profitability and viability of capital-intensive AI business models.
Furthermore, the regulatory landscape remains deeply fractured, adding another layer of uncertainty for investors. A fierce tug-of-war is underway between political leaders advocating for minimal interference and industry voices calling for guardrails. US President Donald Trump has consistently urged limited government regulation to maintain American competitive dominance.
However, IMF chief Georgieva drew a direct line between responsible regulation and sustainable investment. Speaking in Bangkok, she cautioned that a laissez-faire approach could ultimately destroy the very industry it seeks to protect. “If there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities,” she warned, suggesting that public backlash or catastrophic failures stemming from unregulated AI could prompt a draconian regulatory crackdown that would stifle innovation entirely.
The message from Bangkok is clear: the artificial intelligence boom is a double-edged sword. While it has provided a much-needed lifeline to a global economy battered by war and inflation, its sheer scale makes it a potential single point of failure. As policymakers and central bankers look to the future, their challenge is no longer just about fostering innovation, but about engineering a "soft landing" for the AI sector—ensuring that its growth is built on durable profitability and robust safeguards, rather than speculative fervor.

Key Moments
- The People’s Bank of China set the USD/CNY central parity at 6.7138 for Friday’s session, versus 6.7147 previously.
- The new fixing differs from a Reuters estimate of 6.6548 for the same session.
- The PBOC continues to use multiple policy levers, including the Loan Prime Rate, to influence lending costs and the yuan’s exchange rate.
Latest USD/CNY Central Parity Setting
On Friday, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) set the central USD/CNY reference rate for the upcoming trading session at 6.7138. This compares with the prior day’s official fixing of 6.7147 and a Reuters projection of 6.6548 for the same session.
| Fixing Detail | USD/CNY Level | 
|---|---|
| Friday PBOC central rate | 6.7138 | 
| Previous day’s official fix | 6.7147 | 
| Reuters estimate | 6.6548 | 
Mandate and Role of the PBOC
The People’s Bank of China is tasked with maintaining overall price stability, including stability in the exchange rate, while supporting economic growth. As China’s central bank, it also seeks to advance financial reforms, including measures aimed at opening and developing the domestic financial market.
Ownership and Governance Structure
The PBOC is owned by the state of the People’s Republic of China and is therefore not regarded as an independent institution. Oversight and strategic direction are heavily influenced by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) Committee Secretary, who is nominated by the Chairman of the State Council. This post, rather than the governorship alone, plays a central role in shaping the bank’s policy stance. Mr. Pan Gongsheng currently serves in both capacities.
Key Monetary Policy Instruments
The PBOC operates with a wider toolkit than many central banks in Western economies. Its principal policy instruments include:
- Seven-day Reverse Repo operations
- Medium-term Lending Facility (MLF)
- Foreign exchange market interventions
- Reserve Requirement Ratio (RRR) adjustments
China’s Loan Prime Rate (LPR) functions as the benchmark interest rate. Changes to the LPR feed through directly to borrowing costs on loans and mortgages, as well as returns on savings. By adjusting the LPR, the central bank can also exert influence on the Chinese renminbi’s exchange rate.
Presence of Private Banks in China
Private-sector banks are permitted in China, though they represent a relatively small portion of the overall banking system. There are 19 private banks, including major digital lenders WeBank and MYbank, which are backed by Tencent and Ant Group, respectively, according to The Straits Times. In 2014, authorities allowed domestically funded lenders, fully capitalized with private capital, to operate within the predominantly state-controlled financial sector.

articles.title: Lagarde to resign early as ECB holds rates amid inflation concerns - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Lagarde to resign early as ECB holds rates amid inflation concerns  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde has announced she will step down on February 7, 2027, nearly nine months before the end of her term, saying she wants greater freedom to speak about global issues beyond monetary policy.
The announcement came on Thursday (October 29), as the ECB kept its benchmark deposit rate unchanged at 2.5% amid rising inflation, higher energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict and turmoil in European government bond markets, particularly in France.
Lagarde, 70, has led the ECB since November 2019, having previously served as managing director of the International Monetary Fund. Her eight-year term was originally due to end in October 2027.
Speaking at a press conference in Frankfurt, she explained that the political neutrality required of ECB officials had increasingly prevented her from expressing views on wider international developments.
"I don't think that I can remain neutral," Lagarde said.
She explained that she wanted the freedom to express herself and participate in discussions beyond the central bank's monetary policy responsibilities.
Lagarde also expressed concern about misinformation and the distortion of facts, arguing that her experience in international economic and financial institutions could contribute to broader public debate.
She did not specify which issues she intended to address after leaving office.
Lagarde's announcement coincided with an important monetary policy decision, as the ECB left its three main interest rates unchanged following two increases earlier this year.
The deposit rate remained at 2.5%, the main refinancing rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending rate at 2.9%.
Eurozone inflation reached 3.8% in September, almost twice the ECB's medium-term target of 2%, as rising energy costs continued to affect the European economy.
The central bank warned that higher energy prices were increasing inflation risks while threatening economic growth.
The conflict involving Iran has disrupted international energy markets, adding to price pressures across Europe.
Although underlying inflation has remained relatively stable and wage pressures have not increased significantly, policymakers remain concerned that prolonged energy-price increases could eventually spread to other goods, services and wages.
The ECB has therefore left open the possibility of another interest rate increase at its December meeting, although it has not committed to a particular course of action.
The ECB also faces growing concerns over government borrowing costs, particularly in France, where rising bond yields have increased pressure on public finances.
Higher government bond yields can push up borrowing costs for businesses and households, potentially weakening investment, consumption and economic growth.
The central bank faces a difficult balance between controlling inflation and avoiding further pressure on an already vulnerable economy.
France's debt-market difficulties have also raised questions about whether the ECB might need to intervene if borrowing costs rise in a disorderly manner.
However, the central bank has maintained that its market-stabilisation instruments are designed to address disruptions to monetary policy transmission rather than compensate for weaknesses in individual governments' fiscal policies.
Lagarde's decision also comes ahead of France's presidential election in 2027, adding a political dimension to the appointment of her successor.
Her departure in February would allow current European Union leaders to select the next ECB president before the French election.
French President Emmanuel Macron, who will participate in the European decision-making process, thanked Lagarde for her service and called for an orderly transition coordinated with European partners.
However, representatives of Marine Le Pen's National Rally party criticised the timing of her resignation.
Jean-Philippe Tanguy, who is involved in preparing the party's economic policies, questioned the decision, while German European Parliament member Markus Ferber warned that any perception of an appointment being influenced by national electoral considerations could damage confidence in the ECB's independence.
Lagarde did not directly address questions about whether she had deliberately timed her departure to allow the appointment to take place before the French election.
European Council President António Costa confirmed that the process of selecting Lagarde's successor would begin immediately.
Two former central bank governors are widely regarded as leading candidates: Klaas Knot, former president of the Dutch central bank, and Pablo Hernández de Cos, former governor of the Bank of Spain and current general manager of the Bank for International Settlements.
The leadership change could form part of a broader reshuffle of senior ECB positions.
Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel is expected to leave in January, while chief economist Philip Lane's term ends in May.
Financial markets showed little immediate reaction to Lagarde's announcement, with analysts pointing to the ECB's established institutional framework and the experience of potential successors.
There has also been speculation that Lagarde could take up a role at the World Economic Forum, although the organisation has declined to comment.
Despite uncertainty over the leadership transition, Lagarde insisted that her departure would not affect the ECB's ability to make monetary policy decisions.
She said the succession process was already under way and expressed confidence in the institution's strength and stability.
Her decision brings an earlier-than-expected end to a presidency that has spanned the Covid-19 pandemic, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and renewed inflationary pressures linked to the Middle East conflict.
The ECB must now prepare for a leadership transition while continuing to address inflation, rising borrowing costs and broader uncertainty across the eurozone economy.

articles.full_text:
(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices were sharply lower in late U.S. trading Friday, as a technology-led equity market selloff intensified liquidation pressure across precious metals, offsetting the support normally provided by falling Treasury yields and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Crude oil prices climbed more than 2% following another tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz, adding to inflation concerns and expectations that Federal Reserve monetary policy will remain restrictive. Spot gold was trading near $3,879.90 an ounce, down $141.60, or 3.52%, while spot silver was trading near $49.015, down $3.150, or 6.06%, on the session.
Friday's U.S. economic reports presented a mixed picture of moderating wage growth and weakening regional manufacturing activity. The employment cost index increased 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9% in the second quarter. The October Chicago purchasing managers' index declined to 55.3 from 58.8 in September, missing expectations near 56.1 but remaining above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction. Friday's softer wage and manufacturing readings followed Thursday's stronger-than-expected third-quarter gross domestic product report, which showed the U.S. economy expanding at a 3.4% annualized pace, compared with 2.2% in the second quarter. September headline personal consumption expenditures inflation accelerated to 3.6% annually, while core PCE inflation increased to 3.1%, reinforcing concerns about persistent underlying price pressure.
Market positioning remains divided between resilient economic growth, persistent inflation and the growing risk of financial-market instability. The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% Wednesday, with two policymakers favoring an immediate 25-basis-point increase. Interest rate futures continued to reflect substantial expectations for further tightening in December, although Friday's moderating employment costs and sharp equity-market decline provided counterweights to the inflationary implications of strong GDP growth and higher energy prices. Treasury yields fell as investors sought the relative safety of government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year yield retreating toward 4.93% and the two-year yield approaching 4.58%. However, gold continued to decline, suggesting that forced liquidation, portfolio rebalancing and the broader outlook for restrictive monetary policy outweighed immediate safe-haven demand.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a major source of energy-market uncertainty Friday after another commercial tanker was attacked in the strategic waterway. The vessel was struck by explosive devices attached to its hull by a small boat, highlighting the continuing vulnerability of commercial shipping despite regional diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions. Responsibility for the attack had not been established. The incident intensified concerns that renewed military confrontation involving Iran and the United States could further disrupt Middle Eastern energy exports, particularly as markets assessed the possibility of additional military action following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections. Negotiations involving Washington, Tehran and regional mediators have yet to produce a confirmed settlement, leaving disagreements over sanctions, maritime security and the future of commercial access through Hormuz unresolved.
Crude oil futures rose more than 2% Friday, reaching their highest settlements since late April as traders assessed the possibility of renewed disruptions to Gulf energy supplies. December Brent crude futures gained $2.76, or 2.4%, to settle at $117.64 a barrel after reaching $118.00 intraday. The more actively traded January Brent contract advanced $2.63 to $113.43, while Nymex WTI futures increased $2.12, or 2.08%, to settle at $104.12. Brent gained approximately 13.6% during October, while WTI rose 15.2%, reflecting persistent concerns about Middle Eastern supply security and the inflationary consequences of the regional conflict.
For gold, the latest Hormuz attack reinforced underlying geopolitical demand, but higher crude prices also heightened the risk that inflation will remain persistent and the Federal Reserve will maintain restrictive monetary policy. The sharp decline in bullion despite falling Treasury yields indicates that broader financial-market liquidation was the more immediate influence on Friday's trading. Silver suffered considerably greater losses as weakness in precious metals coincided with concerns about industrial demand, equity-market valuations and restrictive financing conditions. The widening gold-silver ratio reflected silver's greater sensitivity to deteriorating risk sentiment and concerns about manufacturing activity.
North American equity markets finished sharply lower Friday as disappointing corporate earnings and concerns about artificial intelligence-related investment triggered heavy selling in technology shares. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined approximately 1.1% to close at 51,770.31, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8% to 7,580.07, its largest daily decline since June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.9% to finish near 25,437, as weakness in semiconductor and major technology shares dominated trading. Intel plunged nearly 29% following disappointing profit guidance, while concerns surrounding Amazon's capital spending added to pressure on the technology sector. The Russell 2000 declined 1.7% to 2,811.84, indicating that selling extended beyond large-cap growth companies. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also fell sharply, losing more than 2% as weakness in precious metals mining and other resource shares compounded the broader deterioration in risk sentiment.
European equity markets closed mostly lower Friday as technology-sector weakness and concerns about elevated energy prices weighed on investor sentiment. The pan-European Stoxx 600 declined approximately 0.4% to 646.73, while Germany's DAX lost 0.9% to finish near 25,819. France's CAC 40 slipped 0.1% to approximately 7,962, while the U.K.'s FTSE 100 outperformed, advancing 0.1% to around 10,736. The Euro Stoxx 50 fell approximately 1.2%, reflecting heavier losses among major continental companies. European technology shares were particularly weak as the U.S. semiconductor selloff affected global valuations, while higher crude prices added to concerns about inflation, corporate margins and the outlook for regional monetary policy. Despite Friday's losses, the Stoxx 600 finished October higher, reflecting gains earlier in the month.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil futures higher and settling at $104.12 a barrel, while December Brent crude futures finished at $117.64. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note declined toward the 4.93% area as demand for government bonds increased during the equity selloff. The U.S. dollar was comparatively firm, supported by defensive demand and expectations for restrictive Federal Reserve policy. articles.full_text:
Key Moments
- EUR/JPY traded around 175.65 in early European hours on Wednesday, staying in negative territory below its 100-day moving average.
- Japanese officials reiterated readiness for decisive FX action, while markets looked ahead to ECB and BoJ policy decisions later in the week.
- Technical signals showed EUR/JPY near lower Bollinger Band support at 175.45, with the RSI at 32.67, pointing to a stretched but intact downside bias.
Euro-Yen Under Pressure as Yen Strengthens
EUR/JPY weakened to roughly 175.65 during early European trading on Wednesday, extending its decline and maintaining a negative tone beneath the 100-day Simple Moving Average (SMA). Bearish momentum in the Relative Strength Index (RSI) reinforced the downside bias as the Japanese Yen (JPY) firmed against the Euro (EUR) on mounting concerns over potential currency-market intervention by Japanese authorities.
The immediate support level for the pair is identified at 175.45, while the first notable resistance on the upside is seen at 176.43.
Japanese Officials Reaffirm Intervention Readiness
Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama stated on Tuesday that the government is prepared to take decisive steps in the foreign-exchange market if needed. Katayama also indicated that authorities will continue to observe market developments with “heightened urgency, including at this moment.”
These comments have contributed to a firmer Yen tone as markets weigh the risk that authorities could act if volatility or depreciation in JPY were to intensify.
Policy Meetings in Focus: ECB and BoJ
Market participants are awaiting the European Central Bank (ECB) interest rate announcement on Thursday, seeking fresh direction for the Euro. Attention will then turn to the Bank of Japan (BoJ) policy decision on Friday.
The ECB had previously increased its three key policy rates by 25 basis points in September. The upcoming decision on Thursday is widely expected to result in unchanged rates, although expectations remain elevated for additional tightening in subsequent meetings, with higher oil prices and persistent inflation risks keeping pressure on policymakers.
The BoJ, for its part, is anticipated to leave its policy rate at 1.25% at the conclusion of its two-day meeting on Friday. According to Reuters reports referenced in the article, the central bank is also expected to state that its “underlying inflation” target of 2% has been achieved, which could carry implications for the pace and extent of future policy normalization.
Analyst Views: Intervention Risk Still Seen at a Distance
Commentary from analysts at MUFG/BTMU suggests that while the possibility of official FX action remains on the table, it is not seen as imminent. They remark that
“we are likely still some distance from that with the 160-level the obvious point in which those threats could turn into action.”
They further note that
“the yen may well struggle through this week with investors likely anticipating BoJ Governor Ueda being more cautious in his words on Friday given the global backdrop.”
MUFG/BTMU analysts also expect the BoJ to recognize the need for additional tightening, but they caution that market expectations may not be fully met. As they put it,
“the BoJ will be mindful of that and while we expect the BoJ to signal more rate hikes are necessary, Ueda’s style of communication suggests he may not provide a strong message on a move in December that remains 80% priced.”
BoJ’s Himino Highlights Inflation Risks and AI-Driven Investment
Comments attributed to BoJ’s Himino, evaluated via the FXS Speechtracker, show a score of 8.2, matching the speaker’s historical average. However, the focus on rising underlying inflation and higher inflation expectations indicates a hawkish leaning. References to strong capital expenditure tied to artificial intelligence, firm export activity, accommodative financial conditions, and fast-growing bank lending underline that real interest rates are still low and that upside inflation risks are gaining prominence.
The signal that delaying policy adjustments could elevate inflation risks and harm the broader economy points to a growing willingness to tighten policy in pursuit of stable prices. From an FX perspective, the combination of underlying inflation near target and heightened upside risks supports expectations for continued normalization, which is viewed as constructive for the Yen, particularly against lower-yielding currencies.
Technical Picture: EUR/JPY Holds Bearish Bias Below 100-Day Average
On the daily chart, EUR/JPY retains a short-term bearish stance, with spot prices trading well beneath the 100-day Moving Average and below the 20-day simple moving average of the Bollinger Bands. The pair is hovering just above the lower Bollinger Band, while the 14-day RSI at 32.67 is close to oversold territory. This combination points to persistent downward pressure, even as the recent decline appears stretched.
| Technical Level | Type | Comment | 
|---|---|---|
| 175.45 | Support | Lower Bollinger Band and first key downside level | 
| 175.10 | Support | October 23 low, exposed if 175.45 breaks | 
| 174.74 | Support | October 6, 2025 low, next level below 175.10 | 
| 176.43 | Resistance | October 26 high, initial upside barrier | 
| 177.00 | Resistance | Approximate middle Bollinger Band area | 
| 178.50 | Resistance | Upper Bollinger Band, key cap before psychological 180.00 | 
| 180.00 | Resistance | Psychological level, above upper band | 
| 182.20 | Resistance | 100-day Moving Average | 
On the downside, a decisive move below the lower Bollinger Band at 175.45 would open the way for a test of the October 23 trough at 175.10, with further weakness then targeting the October 6, 2025 low at 174.74.
On the topside, initial resistance is located at the October 26 peak of 176.43. A recovery above that area would bring the Bollinger middle band near 177.00 into view, followed by the upper Bollinger boundary around 178.50. Sustained buying beyond 178.50 could clear the path toward the psychological 180.00 mark and ultimately the 100-day Moving Average at 182.20.

articles.full_text:
- Dollar steady against FX rivals
- Buck’s gauge holds above 102.40
- Fed expected to hold interest rates flat
Greenback retains its gains despite the recovery in stocks, with traders watching whether the Fed reinforces expectations for another rate increase.
💵 Dollar strength survives the rally
- The US dollar index DXY held near 102.40 Wednesday, its highest level since October 14, after gaining 0.3% Tuesday.
- Traders are awaiting the Federal Reserve’s decision later today. A pause is widely expected, putting greater emphasis on what policymakers say about the possibility of further tightening in December.
- The recovery in equities has not displaced demand for the dollar. With US 10-year Treasury yields near 5%, dollar assets continue to offer substantial income.
- DXY measures the dollar against six currencies, with the euro carrying 57.6% of the total weight. That makes developments in Europe particularly influential: euro weakness can lift the index even when the dollar is mixed elsewhere.
🌍 Major currencies face separate tests
- EUR/USD traded near $1.1120 and GBP/USD around $1.33 in early Wednesday trading. The euro has faced pressure from expensive energy, French fiscal concerns and volatility in government bonds.
- Thursday’s ECB decision will help determine whether Europe’s interest-rate outlook provides enough support to challenge the dollar’s recent advantage.
- USD/JPY hovered near ¥157.90, while USD/CAD traded around C$1.4060 in early-session moves. Both pairs face additional domestic catalysts: the Bank of Canada announces its decision at 9:45 a.m. ET today, followed by the BOJ on Friday.
- New Zealand showed how sharply expectations can move FX. NZD/USD fell as much as 2% to $0.5570 after the RBNZ unexpectedly held rates at 2.75%. Australia moved differently: AUD/USD edged toward $0.7035 following firm inflation data.
🏦 Fed guidance sets the next direction
- Futures pricing indicated roughly a 91% probability of unchanged Fed rates. With that outcome largely anticipated, the announcement at 2 p.m. ET could move currencies through guidance alone.
- A stronger commitment to further tightening could support the dollar; softer language could prompt investors to unwind positions built around December hike expectations.
- The Fed will not settle the outlook for long. US GDP and September PCE inflation arrive Thursday at 8:30 a.m. ET, alongside the ECB decision later that morning.
- Firm inflation could reinforce expectations for restrictive policy, while softer readings could weaken the dollar’s yield support. Friday’s BOJ decision adds another potential catalyst for the heavily watched yen pair.
