articles.title: Piero Cipollone: Next-day securities settlement, tokenisation and the transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure
articles.full_text:
- SPEECH
Next-day securities settlement, tokenisation and the transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure
Keynote address by Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at an EU T+1 Industry Committee event on “One year to T+1”
Frankfurt am Main, 29 October 2026
We are approaching an important milestone.[1]
Less than a year from now, on 11 October 2027, Europe will move to T+1 settlement. This means that the time from the moment a security is traded to the moment the buyer receives it and the seller is paid will be reduced from two days to one.
This may sound like a technical change, but it is in fact much more significant.
The transition to T+1 is part of a broader transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure. And the objective is clear: to make Europe’s financial and payment system more efficient, more resilient and safer, and ultimately to make European financial markets more competitive.
In the Eurosystem, we are contributing to this transformation across the full spectrum of our mandate.
We are ensuring that banknotes remain available and fit for purpose. We are preparing for a digital euro. We are modernising wholesale payments and securities settlement. And we are working to enhance cross-border payments and harness new technologies such as distributed ledger technology (DLT).[2]
These are not separate projects. They are different parts of the same strategy: ensuring that the euro and Europe’s financial markets are fit for the future in a rapidly changing world.
From T+2 to T+1: an essential element of a broader modernisation effort
The move to T+1 contributes to this broader strategy.
It is about more than just reducing the time between trade and settlement to one day.
A shorter settlement cycle can reduce market and counterparty risk.
But, perhaps even more importantly for Europe, the transition is also forcing us to review our post-trade processes. It requires greater standardisation, automation and innovation. Inefficiencies that could be accommodated in a T+2 environment will become much more difficult to sustain under T+1.
In that sense, T+1 is a catalyst for modernising European post-trade markets. And this is important for Europe’s competitiveness.
Efficient post-trade infrastructure makes it easier for capital to flow across borders. It helps investors access European markets. And it supports the EU’s wider ambition to create deeper and more integrated capital markets.
It also ensures that Europe keeps pace internationally with other major markets as they shorten their own settlement cycles.
That is why the ECB, together with the European Securities and Markets Authority and the European Commission, strongly supports the market’s preparations for T+1.
There is another lesson for Europe here which I believe is particularly important: we can deliver when we work together.
Europe’s financial landscape remains complex and fragmented. Yet the work coordinated by the EU T+1 Industry Committee has shown that those differences do not need to stand in the way of common solutions.
I would therefore like to congratulate everyone involved for the progress made so far. It is a powerful reminder of what Europe can achieve when public authorities and the private sector come together around a common objective.
But we have not yet crossed the finish line.
The coming months will be critical. Implementation and testing need to advance with the same determination and cooperation that have been the driving force behind the project so far.
The Eurosystem is also responsible for operating TARGET2-Securities (T2S), our platform for securities settlement in central bank money through which cash and securities can be exchanged simultaneously across Europe.[3]
And the key message here is a simple one: T2S already supports shorter settlement cycles. It already settles substantial volumes of transactions on a T+1 and even a T+0 basis.
So we are not starting from scratch.
At the same time, we are adapting some T2S processes to help the market operate efficiently under the tighter timetable that T+1 will bring. This includes changes to the night-time settlement process, which are planned for June 2027 ahead of the market’s migration to T+1 settlement in October 2027.
We will continue working closely with market participants and other European authorities to ensure that the transition to T+1 settlement goes smoothly.
Preparing for the financial system of tomorrow
But while we prepare for T+1, we also need to look further ahead.
Technology is reshaping finance. Distributed ledger technology and tokenisation offer opportunities not only to make today’s processes faster by enabling the near-instant transfer of securities, but potentially to simplify the architecture of finance itself. Tokenisation could bring issuance, trading, clearing, settlement, custody and asset servicing into a shared digital environment.
The Eurosystem intends to be part of that transformation, and we have already moved from vision to delivery.[4]
Since 30 March, the Eurosystem has been accepting marketable assets issued in central securities depositories using distributed ledger technology as eligible collateral for its credit operations.[5] We are now assessing whether, how and under what criteria DLT-based assets outside currently eligible settlement systems could become eligible collateral. We will ensure that our collateral framework keeps pace with innovation while upholding our statutory requirement for collateral to be adequate.
Since 21 September, Pontes has enabled wholesale transactions in tokenised assets to be settled in central bank money. It connects market DLT platforms with our TARGET Services, bringing the safety of central bank money to the emerging world of tokenised finance.[6]
To further build on this momentum, the Eurosystem will enhance the initial core functionalities of Pontes. We will do so in steps, for example by extending the operating hours significantly by mid-2027 and moving to 24/7/365 availability in 2028. We also plan to offer immediate settlement finality on the Eurosystem DLT platform as early as next year.
Appia looks further ahead.
It is exploring how we can build an integrated European ecosystem for tokenised finance around common standards, with central bank money continuing to provide the anchor of trust and stability.
By 2028, Appia aims to deliver a blueprint setting out key findings, recommendations and principles for a safe, innovative and integrated European tokenised financial ecosystem.[7]
Yesterday we published a report on the outcome of the public consultation on the Appia roadmap.[8] The consultation confirmed broad market support for developing an integrated, innovative and resilient European tokenised finance ecosystem anchored in central bank money. It also revealed a high degree of willingness among respondents to contribute actively to Appia. This provides a strong basis to develop Appia as a public-private partnership.
But embracing the future does not mean discarding what already works.
So, what does all this mean for T2S?
Let me be very clear: T2S is not going to disappear any time soon.
Different technologies and infrastructures will coexist because they are suited to different functions and different use cases.
T2S will continue to serve European securities markets. At the same time, tokenised platforms will develop and new forms of financial market infrastructure will emerge. The Eurosystem’s tokenisation strategy therefore complements our continuous efforts to improve and modernise our existing TARGET Services.
So we should not frame the discussion as a choice between today’s infrastructure and tomorrow’s technology.
The real challenge is to enable them to coexist.
We need existing and new infrastructures to work together effectively, while preserving the safety of settlement in central bank money and avoiding the emergence of new technological silos.
Innovation should help Europe overcome fragmentation – it shouldn’t recreate that fragmentation in digital form.
Conclusion
Let me conclude.
T+1, T2S, Pontes and Appia may appear to be different initiatives.
But they are connected by a common purpose.
We want Europe’s financial infrastructure to be robust and resilient. We want it to be efficient and innovative. And we want it to provide a foundation on which an integrated and competitive European financial market can develop.
T+1 will be an important step on that journey.
We now have less than a year to complete the transition.
So let us keep up the momentum, intensify implementation and testing, and make Europe’s transition to T+1 a success.
Thank you.
- I would like to thank Rémy Al Sbinati, Maria Foskolou, Gergely Kóczán, Lucia Martin Moran, Karoun Meresené and Anna Nuzzolo for their help in preparing this speech.
- See Lagarde, C. (2026), “Money in transition”, opening speech at the ECB conference on “Money in transition: digitalisation and innovation in payments”, Frankfurt am Main, 15 June.
- See “What is T2S?” on the ECB’s website.
- Cipollone, P. (2026), “From vision to delivery: building Europe’s tokenised financial market”, speech at the Deutsche Bundesbank’s Symposium on “Future of payments: trends and innovations in Germany and Europe”, Frankfurt am Main, 26 August.
- ECB (2026), “ECB paves way for acceptance of DLT-based assets as eligible Eurosystem collateral”, press release, 27 January.
- ECB (2026), “Eurosystem brings central bank money to tokenised finance”, press release, 21 September.
- ECB (2026), Appia – paving the way for a future-ready, integrated financial ecosystem leveraging tokenisation and DLT, 11 March.
- ECB (2026), Eurosystem report on the public consultation on the Appia Roadmap, 28 October.

articles.title: Inflation heats up again, days before midterm elections - PBS
articles.summary: Inflation heats up again, days before midterm elections  PBSInflation Accelerated in October, PCE Index Shows  The New York TimesLast snapshot of the US economy before midterms shows stronger growth but higher inflation  CNNSeptember PCE Report: PCE Inflation Index Up 3.6%, in Line with Expectations  MorningstarStocks Down Pre-Bell Ahead of Key Inflation Report, Amazon Earnings  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — An inflation gauge closely monitored by the Federal Reserve accelerated last month, showing that prices remain elevated less than a week before midterm elections in which the uncomfortably high cost of living for millions of Americans has become a central issue.
Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May.
Rising gas prices drove much of the inflation increase as renewed violence in the Middle East has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, up from below $70 before the Iran war. But prices also rose outside of fuel costs. The cost of services such as shipping, hotel rooms, and utilities increased rapidly from August to September, a sign that inflation is spreading and growing more entrenched.
"The inflation outlook has become more concerning," Ksenia Bushmeneva, an economist at TD, a bank, wrote in a commentary on the report. "Price pressures are showing signs of heating up. Elevated gasoline prices are keeping headline inflation hot, but underlying pressures are also broadening."
Polls show that the rise in inflation has soured most voters on the economy, leading them to give President Donald Trump poor marks on handling rising prices. Trump campaigned in 2024 on lowering the cost of living, including bringing the cost of gas below $2 a gallon. It currently averages about $4.25 a gallon nationwide.
Excluding the volatile energy and food categories, core inflation also picked up last month. It increased 3.1% from a year ago in September, up from 3% in August, the Commerce Department said. And from August to September, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the previous month.
Separately, the government also said the economy grew at a strong 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, much faster than the 2.2% growth in the April-June quarter, as consumer spending jumped and business investment rose, fueled by spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Consumer spending climbed 3.8% at an annual rate in the third quarter, the second straight quarter of strong growth and far above the 0.7% increase in the first three months of the year.
Yet there are signs that consumers may struggle to maintain that level of spending. Inflation is eroding their incomes: In September, inflation-adjusted incomes, after taxes, declined 0.3% from the previous month. Consumers appear to be dipping into savings or relying on credit to fuel much of their consumption.
"Together with higher borrowing costs, these headwinds are likely to weigh on consumer demand in the coming quarters," Bushmeneva said."
The reports come a day after the Federal Reserve, the agency tasked with combatting inflation, left its key interest rate unchanged. Yet strong economic growth and persistently higher prices could mean more pain for Americans when the Fed meets in December. The Fed is much more likely to hike its key interest rate, which could lift borrowing costs across the economy.
Thursday's inflation data comes from the personal consumption expenditures price index, which typically echoes the better-known consumer price index published earlier this month. The Fed more closely monitors the PCE index because it puts less weight on housing prices and allows for changes in consumers' shopping habits.

articles.title: Fed rate hold offers little comfort to Indian markets as two members seek a hike - TradingView
articles.summary: Fed rate hold offers little comfort to Indian markets as two members seek a hike  TradingView
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged may offer some near-term relief to Indian equities, but two policymakers voting for a rate hike are expected to keep concerns over global liquidity and foreign investor flows alive.
The Fed on Wednesday kept its benchmark federal funds rate unchanged at 3.75-4 per cent in a 10-2 vote, as widely expected. Governors Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack favoured a 25-basis-point increase, signalling concerns over persistent inflation even as the central bank chose to wait for more economic data.
The dissenting votes mean investors cannot interpret the pause as a clear signal that the rate-tightening cycle has ended, market experts said. The possibility of another hike in December could keep global bond yields and the dollar under pressure, influencing foreign portfolio investor flows into emerging markets such as India.
“While the US Federal Reserve has kept interest rates unchanged at 3.75-4 per cent, the decision is not necessarily a dovish signal for global equity markets,” said Thomas Priju, portfolio manager at Karma Capital. “A further increase in US interest rates could keep US bond yields and the dollar elevated, putting pressure on emerging-market capital flows and increasing volatility in the Nifty.”
High-valuation stocks and companies dependent on foreign portfolio flows could be particularly sensitive to changes in global liquidity, Priju said.
However, the dissenting votes do not necessarily mean that a rate hike in December is certain. The Fed has left its next move dependent on incoming inflation and economic data, while the timing of any further increase will determine how global markets respond.
Economic strength
The Fed upgraded its assessment of US economic activity from “solid” to “strong”, while reiterating that inflation remains elevated. Its statement said that gathering more information would help policymakers determine the appropriate policy stance to return inflation to its 2 per cent target.
Geopolitical developments and the ongoing quarterly earnings season are also expected to remain important drivers of stock-specific and broader market performance, experts said.
Umesh Sharma, chief investment officer for debt at The Wealth Company Mutual Fund, said the combination of the two hawkish dissents, stronger economic growth language and the absence of clear forward guidance kept the possibility of a December hike alive. He said that incoming inflation and growth data could drive volatility in US Treasury yields, with spillover effects on Indian government securities.
Investors will also track policy decisions by the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan this week, alongside developments in US inflation and the November 3 midterm elections, they said. For Indian equities, the direction of foreign fund flows, the rupee and domestic earnings is expected to help determine how much of the uncertainty around US rates is reflected in market prices.

articles.title: De-Dollarization but for the Lack of an Alternative - GoldSeek
articles.summary: De-Dollarization but for the Lack of an Alternative  GoldSeek
articles.full_text:
Central banks are actively diversifying their foreign exchange reserves away from the U.S. dollar.
Dedollarization refers to a strategic economic process where governments, central banks, and market participants reduce their reliance on the U.S. dollar (USD) for international trade, foreign exchange reserves, and bilateral transactions.
For decades, the U.S. dollar has served as the world’s primary global reserve currency. Dedollarization occurs when countries actively shift toward alternative currencies (like the Euro, Chinese Yuan, or local currencies) or tangible assets (like gold) to settle debts and store national wealth.
Countries typically pursue dedollarization due to a combination of geopolitical, strategic, and macroeconomic factors:
The weaponization of the USD financial system (such as freezing central bank reserves or disconnecting nations from the SWIFT network) pushes sidelined nations to find alternative payment rails.
Relying entirely on one currency exposes global economies to domestic U.S. monetary policy changes, inflation, and political instability.
As emerging economies grow, blocks like BRICS actively promote utilizing local currencies for cross-border trade to bypass USD conversion costs.
To track the progress of dedollarization, economists measure the dollar’s share across three primary pillars: Foreign Exchange Reserves, Global Trade Invoicing, and International Debt/Liquidity.
While the USD’s share in central bank reserves has gradually decreased over the last two decades, it still maintains a dominant lead in global payments and trade.
Understanding what dedollarization isn’t helps clarify its actual impact on the global stage:
It is a slow, structural shift playing out over decades, rather than a sudden displacement of the U.S. financial system.
The goal for most nations is diversification and autonomy, not a complete ban on holding or trading in USD.
No single currency currently possesses the liquidity, open capital markets, and legal protections required to fully replace the USD as a singular global standard.
Historical precedent
The most striking historical precedent for modern de-dollarization is the transition of the global reserve currency from the British Pound Sterling (GBP) to the U.S. Dollar (USD) during the 20th century.
For nearly a century, the British pound was the undisputed anchor of international commerce. Its displacement was not a sudden overnight collapse, but a gradual multi-decade process driven by war, shifting macroeconomic power, and heavy debt accumulation.
By the late 1800s, Great Britain’s Industrial Revolution had made London the undisputed center of global trade and finance.
The vast majority of global trade was invoiced in pounds, and central banks held their wealth in sterling because it was directly convertible to gold.
Even though the U.S. economy surpassed Britain’s in size by the 1880s, the pound maintained its reserve status. This highlights how “inertia” keeps a legacy currency dominant long after an economy has been eclipsed
The structural shift began in earnest with World War I.
To finance the war, Britain borrowed heavily from the United States, transitioning from a global creditor to a debtor nation.
While Britain had to temporarily suspend its gold standard to pay for the war, the U.S. dollar remained continuously tied to gold. By the mid-1920s, the U.S. dollar was openly competing with and occasionally surpassing the pound in central bank reserve holdings.
World War II dealt the final economic blow to Britain’s currency empire. Severely depleted by the war, Great Britain could no longer sustain its global financial architecture.
Conclusion
There are several striking similarities between the challenges facing the U.S. dollar today and the conditions that triggered the decline of the British pound. However, there are also structural differences that make a total dollar collapse unlikely anytime soon.
Economists point to clear parallels in skyrocketing national debt and geopolitical friction, balanced by a major difference: the modern dollar lacks a clear, single successor like the U.S. was to Britain.
Following the World Wars, Great Britain suffered from deep structural financial imbalances. Today, the United States is facing a massive expansion of national debt, with gross federal debt exceeding $40 trillion and a gross debt-to-GDP ratio standing at about 126%. Net interest payments consume nearly 15% of all federal spending, mirroring the fiscal strain that historically weakened the pound.
Just as the global economy fragmented into the British-led “Sterling Area” and outside markets, modern geopolitics is seeing a clear divide. The weaponization of the dollar via aggressive financial sanctions (such as freezing Russia’s central bank reserves in 2022) has forced rival blocs like BRICS to build independent cross-border payment solutions to protect their financial sovereignty.
The pound didn’t vanish instantly; it gradually lost ground. The U.S. dollar is currently tracking a similar pattern. The IMF’s Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves shows the dollar’s share of global reserves hovering at roughly 56.7%, down significantly from around 70% in 2000.
While the structural vulnerabilities align, the global landscape looks different in one vital way: the lack of a single, scalable alternative.
Today’s conditions match the internal decay that ruined the pound, mainly unsustainable debt and geopolitical overreach. However, because the rest of the world has no trusted, highly liquid, single alternative to turn to, the dollar’s erosion remains a slow, fragmented drift rather than a sudden displacement.

articles.full_text:
The Morning Bull - UK Market Morning Update Thursday, 29 Oct 2026
UK stocks look set for a softer open, with sentiment dominated by a fresh inflation warning from the High Street. The key issue is simple: shop prices are rising faster again, just as investors were leaning on a cooling inflation story.
UK shop price inflation reached 2.1% year on year in October, compared with 1.4% in September. Food prices rose 2.9%, while non food inflation registered 1.7%. This combination points to broader price pressure, not just isolated items at the checkout.
When price growth re-accelerates, investors tend to reassess interest rate expectations. Higher inflation can keep borrowing costs elevated for longer, which usually weighs on profit expectations for debt heavy businesses and squeezes disposable income sensitive sectors.
The unresolved question now is how the Bank of England reacts as budget announcements approach. If shop price data feeds into a tougher policy stance, the current cautious mood could harden; a softer tone would instead reopen the debate on rate relief.
Stocks to Watch Before the Opening Bell
Rolls-Royce Holdings (RR.)
The UK government has pledged up to £1.25b to Rolls-Royce for its UltraFan short haul jet engine programme, alongside the group’s own £2.5b decade long investment plan. The project targets around 3,300 UK jobs by 2029. Watch how management phases spending and updates on certification, since timelines can affect cash needs and partnership terms.
Rio Tinto Group (RIO)
Rio Tinto has inaugurated its Fénix 1B and Sal de Vida lithium projects in Argentina after around US$1.4b of investment. Both sites have started output ahead of plan and are scaling toward 25,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent capacity. The World Bank’s higher copper price outlook also keeps attention on Rio’s exposure to energy transition metals and future capital allocation.
HUTCHMED (China) (HCM)
HUTCHMED has received US FDA Orphan Drug Designation for sovleplenib in primary immune thrombocytopenia, which brings potential US incentives including 7 years of market exclusivity if approved. New Drug Applications for sovleplenib in primary ITP and warm antibody autoimmune hemolytic anemia are under review in China. Investors will focus on regulatory timetables and any partnership news around this asset.
Top Movers
Rank Group (LSE:RNK) jumped 11.66% as mid cap leisure stocks such as Rank Group outperformed in London trading.
Whitbread (LSE:WTB) climbed 5.59% after shareholder Corvex welcomed proxy support for James Gemmel joining the Whitbread board.
SSE (LSE:SSE) advanced 4.58%.
Top Losers
Hunting (LSE:HTG) fell 9.52% after trimming 2026 EBITDA guidance on weaker Middle East and North America activity.
Dar Global (LSE:DAR) declined 6.63% following updates on its expanded global real estate investment focus centred on Dubai.
Vistry Group (LSE:VTY) dropped 5.87% after recent gains linked to the CFO appointment unwound into profit taking.
On The Radar
Over the next few sessions the UK market is pinned between fresh Bank of England signals and a heavy run of domestic bank and consumer facing results.
BoE Consumer Credit, Thu 29 Oct. A print above the £2.2b consensus would underline resilient borrowing even as shop price inflation runs at 2.1%, which can complicate the case for near term UK rate relief.
UK Mortgage Approvals and Mortgage Lending, Thu 29 Oct. Figures above the 54k approvals and £4.2b to £4.5b lending markers would point to a firmer housing pulse that can keep pressure on rate expectations and rate sensitive domestically focused stocks.
Lloyds Banking Group, Thu 29 Oct. Q3 2026 numbers at 7:00 AM UTC matter most for net interest income and credit quality, since this bank is tightly linked to the UK mortgage and consumer credit cycle.
Shell, Thu 29 Oct. Q3 2026 earnings at 7:00 AM UTC put the focus on cash generation and capital returns, which can sway sentiment across London listed energy producers tied to global oil and gas prices.
BoE Interest Rate Decision, Thu 5 Nov. The move relative to the current 3.75% rate and the market consensus of 4% will feed directly into pricing for UK banks, housebuilders and any equity where valuations lean on lower discount rates.
Sector & Industry Watch
Energy – Strong year, mixed company signals
Energy has edged higher over the past week and remains one of the stronger UK sectors so far this year. Shell is adding output through existing Gulf of America infrastructure, while Hunting just cut its 2026 profit guidance after softer activity in Saudi Arabia and North America.
If you hold oil related stocks, the main near term swing factor is how global crude prices react to incoming US inflation and growth data, because that feeds straight into cash generation for UK listed producers and your fuel costs.
Banks – Tax change meets rate uncertainty
Banks have declined over the last seven days and over the past month, lagging the wider Financials group. Recent news has been mixed, with Standard Chartered lifting its outlook after stronger profits, while the sector adjusts to a higher 6% UK bank surcharge and fresh shop price inflation at 2.1%.
If you own banking stocks, today’s Bank of England consumer credit and mortgage approvals figures are the key check on how households are coping with higher day to day prices and still elevated borrowing costs.
Real Estate – Gentle climb, housing data in focus
Real Estate has moved higher over the past week and month, outpacing the slightly softer GB Market in the short term. Activity around SEGRO, where a large asset manager has disclosed a sizeable stake, suggests big investors remain engaged even as housing exposed groups such as BRCK Group flag pressure from slower building and inflation.
For property heavy portfolios, today’s UK mortgage approvals and mortgage lending data will show whether this recent rise in listed landlords and house related plays fits with actual buyer demand and available credit.
Food, Beverage & Tobacco has gained over the past week and month, at a time when UK shop price inflation has picked up to 2.1% and food inflation runs higher still. Companies such as Unilever and Diageo are leaning on brands and premium launches, while MicroSalt is pushing low sodium ingredients that line up with health and regulatory trends.
If you hold supermarkets or branded food and drink stocks, the thing to watch next is how upcoming trading statements describe UK volumes and promotions into Christmas, because that will show whether shoppers are trading down or absorbing higher shelf prices.
Pharmaceuticals & Biotech – Stock specific swings around trial news
Pharmaceuticals & Biotech has inched higher over the past week, although individual shares are moving sharply on news. GSK fell after weaker vaccine sales and a cautious earnings outlook, while HUTCHMED secured US FDA Orphan Drug Designation for sovleplenib and Ondine Biomedical reported encouraging Phase 3 infection data.
If healthcare is a meaningful slice of your holdings, focus on upcoming company commentary about pricing and research spending, since that will show how management teams balance cost pressure with funding new treatments in the current UK inflation backdrop.

articles.full_text:
After a year of record-breaking gains, the market's tides may be turning. As of this writing, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES: ^DJI), and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) have slipped around 2%, 3%, and 5%, respectively, from their highs earlier this year.
Investor sentiment is also stumbling. The Fear and Greed Index measures investor sentiment on a scale from 0 to 100, with lower values indicating fearful investor behavior and higher figures suggesting greed. As of this writing, the index sits at just 32 -- well into the "fear" category.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
We know that a downturn is bound to happen sooner or later, as no bull market can last forever. But are we on the verge of a recession right now? Here's what the data says.
A nearly flawless recession indicator
The yield curve is one of the most well-known and reliable recession indicators. It inverts when long-term interest rates fall below short-term rates, and an inverted yield curve has preceded nearly every recession since the 1970s.
The 10-year-to-two-year spread is the curve most analysts watch as a recession indicator. Ahead of the dot-com bubble, this curve inverted in February 2000. Just one month later, the dot-com bear market officially began. It inverted again in 2006, and by late 2007, the U.S. was descending into the Great Recession.
Most recently, the yield curve inverted in 2022. While we technically didn't experience a recession that year, stocks fell into a bear market amid economic strain marked by runaway inflation and repeated interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.
10-2 Year Treasury Yield Spread data by YCharts
Right now, the yield curve is not inverted and hasn't been since 2024. But it is sloping downward, and with more interest rate hikes on the table from the Fed, it's uncertain how it will fare going forward.
To be clear, no recession indicator will be 100% correct. Even the more accurate ones can't predict when a downturn will begin, how long it might last, or how severe it might be. That said, history says that it's simpler than you might think to prepare for a potential recession.
How investors can prepare for a recession
We're bound to face some sort of downturn eventually, as recessions are a normal part of the market's cycle. So rather than getting caught up in when it might happen, it's wise to start preparing for the inevitable slump.

articles.title: MPC Preview: November interest rate hike inevitable, the question now is how many more - RSM UK
articles.summary: MPC Preview: November interest rate hike inevitable, the question now is how many more  RSM UK
articles.full_text:
The Bank of England (BoE) is likely to join the global rate-hiking cycle when it meets next week, even if it is a little late to the party. The more interesting question is what happens next. Until recently, the BoE faced an uncomfortable trade-off between tackling inflation and supporting a weak economy. That trade-off has largely disappeared.
Growth has been stronger than expected, the labour market is improving and higher energy prices are pushing inflation further above target. With fewer reasons to wait, we expect the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) to raise rates from 3.75% to 4.00% on 5 November, with a 7–2 vote in favour of a hike and a substantially more hawkish message.
We expect another 25-basis-point increase in February, taking rates to 4.25%. But that is where we part company with markets. Our base case is that inflation will peak and growth will slow sufficiently enough for the Bank to keep rates on hold for the rest of 2027. Unless energy prices rise much further, or higher inflation feeds more clearly into wages, we think markets are overestimating how far interest rates will ultimately need to rise.
Why the Bank of England is set to raise interest rates in November
Almost all the evidence since the MPC’s last meeting points to a rate hike next week.
Higher energy prices pushed inflation to 3.5% in September, 0.5 percentage points above the MPC’s July forecast. We now expect inflation to rise above 4.5% in the new year, slightly higher than in the MPC’s adverse scenario.
Granted, the MPC does not need to respond mechanically to higher energy prices, particularly as higher energy bills squeeze households’ real incomes and, in turn, drag on growth. However, we think the case for looking through the shock is now much weaker.
UK economic growth and stabilising labour market strengthens the case for higher interest rates
The economy has been much stronger than the MPC expected. GDP grew by 0.1% in August and is likely to have expanded by around 0.7% in Q3, comfortably above the MPC’s September forecast of 0.4%. In addition, the PMI rose from 52.0 to 53.1 in October, suggesting that growth will hold up in Q4 rather than slow to a crawl. This sustained improvement suggests that monetary policy may be less restrictive than the MPC previously assumed.
What is more, stronger growth is now feeding through to hiring. The unemployment rate fell from 4.9% to 4.7% in August, payrolls rose by 13,000 in September and the employment PMI climbed above 50 for the first time in more than two years in October. Taken together, these indicators suggest that the labour market is stable or even improving.
That combination of resilient demand and a firmer labour market raises the risk of second-round effects. Firms will find it easier to pass higher costs on to customers, while workers will be in a stronger position to bargain for higher wages.
Indeed, MPC member Megan Greene recently stated that “our broad range of wage indicators suggest there is less slack in the labour market than we thought (...) this suggests the risk of second-round effects taking hold is higher.”
If second-round effects materialise, inflation will remain elevated for longer. We therefore think the MPC will raise rates in November to help limit their emergence and avoid falling behind the curve.
Taken together, higher inflation and a stronger economy mean the MPC currently faces no trade-off between tackling inflation and supporting growth. It has therefore run out of reasons to justify another hold.
We expect a hawkish pivot, with a 7–2 vote in favour of a 25-basis-point hike in November.
How high could UK interest rates go in 2027?
Inflation accelerating to above 4.5% early next year will cement the case for another rate hike in 2027, probably in February, taking interest rates to 4.25%. Our base case is that inflation will have peaked by February and growth will have slowed significantly, allowing the MPC to keep rates on hold for the rest of the year.
There was very little in yesterday’s Budget that the MPC will need to factor in. The measures announced will reduce inflation next year by around 0.1–0.2 percentage points, but that is inconsequential in the context of inflation rising above 4.5%. What is more, slightly looser fiscal policy over the next couple of years would, if anything, be mildly hawkish. Overall, the Budget did nothing to change the outlook for rates over the next year.
Energy prices remain the key risk to the interest rate outlook
Of course, much of the outlook beyond February depends on what happens over the winter. A further rise in energy prices, especially natural gas prices, would probably lead us to factor in a third hike next year. Likewise, evidence that higher inflation was being reflected in pay deals would also make a third hike more likely.
However, we doubt the Bank will need to raise rates to almost 5%, as markets currently expect. Admittedly, current pricing includes a premium for the risk of further increases in energy prices, but we think it would take a much larger rise than currently anticipated to push interest rates that high.
UK interest rate outlook: what happens next?
A rate hike next week looks nailed on. Stronger growth and a falling unemployment rate mean there is no longer a trade-off between supporting a weak economy and tackling high inflation. That makes the decision relatively straightforward for the MPC. The latest surge in energy prices has also removed the luxury of waiting and means there is likely to be at least one additional rate hike next year.

articles.title: China's yuan hits 4-year high versus dollar after Fed decision - Business Recorder
articles.summary: China's yuan hits 4-year high versus dollar after Fed decision  Business Recorder
articles.full_text:
- Prior to market opening, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) set the midpoint rate at 6.7147 per dollar
China's yuan hit a four-year high against the dollar and trading partners after the Fed held rates. China's central bank is actively managing the currency's appreciation, influencing its daily guidance.
- Yuan's four-year high against the dollar and trading partners.
- Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates unchanged.
- China's central bank strategy for managing yuan appreciation.
SHANGHAI: China’s yuan hit a four-year high against the dollar and its major trading partners on Thursday after the Federal Reserve kept rates unchanged, with China’s central bank continuing to guide an orderly appreciation of the currency.
The Fed held interest rates steady, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections while it awaits further data on inflation, which the central bank said “remains elevated.”
Prior to market opening, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) set the midpoint rate at 6.7147 per dollar, its strongest since February 2, 2023. The spot yuan is allowed to trade a maximum of 2% either side of the fixed midpoint each day.
Thursday’s midpoint was 551 pips weaker than a Reuters estimate of 6.6596 — its largest weak-side deviation since September 15.
The central bank has been gradually strengthening its daily yuan official guidance this year, but at levels weaker than market expectations, suggesting it is seeking to manage the pace of appreciation, traders and analysts said.
“PBOC continues to allow the current direction of travel to continue, whilst reining in the pace of the USD/CNY decline,” Maybank analysts said in a note.
In the spot market, the onshore yuan strengthened to a high of 6.6620 per dollar at one point, the strongest since June 7, 2022, before changing hands at 6.6621 as of 0235 GMT.
Its offshore counterpart traded at 6.6601 per dollar, up about 0.03% in Asian trade.
Based on Thursday’s midpoint, the yuan’s trade-weighted value against its major trading partners, as measured by the yuan CFETS basket index, rose to 103.75, the highest since July 15, 2022, according to Reuters calculations based on the official data.
It has gained about 5.9% so far this year, during which the yuan rose about 5% versus the greenback.
Currency traders said they will switch their attention to the European Central Bank policy decision due later in the session, even though it is widely expected to leave rates unchanged.

articles.title: US Fed keeps rates unchanged; what it means for Indian equity market - Fortune India
articles.summary: US Fed keeps rates unchanged; what it means for Indian equity market  Fortune India
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at 3.75%-4.00% in a 10-2 FOMC vote, with two members favoring a 25-basis-point hike. Experts warn the decision offers limited relief for Indian equities, as US inflation remains above target at 3.7% CPI, a December rate hike appears likely, and 10-year Treasury yields hover near 5.02%. Elevated crude oil prices, with Brent near $114.50 per barrel, add further pressure on India's rupee and import bill, potentially constraining foreign portfolio inflows.
- US Fed kept rates unchanged, but future hikes are still possible due to persistent inflation.
- A split vote within the FOMC highlights internal disagreement on monetary policy.
- Tight global liquidity and high US bond yields could limit foreign capital inflows into India.
- Elevated crude oil prices pose an additional risk, potentially increasing India's import bill.
- Indian markets may remain volatile, influenced by global monetary policy and geopolitical risks.
US Fed Rate Hike
- The US Federal Reserve implemented a rate hike, preceding the current decision to hold rates steady.
FOMC Dot Plot Projections
- The FOMC's dot plot projected US inflation returning to the 2% target only by 2029, a year later than previously expected.
US Fed Holds Interest Rates
- The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to maintain the benchmark federal funds rate at 3.75%-4.00%.
US Midterm Elections
- Markets are expected to monitor potential volatility ahead of the upcoming US midterm elections.
Potential Rate Hike Anticipated
- Market experts anticipate a likely US Fed rate hike in December, aligning with projections from the September dot plot.
Projected Inflation Target Return
- The US Fed's September policy indicated inflation is projected to return to its 2% target by this year.
The target interest rate set by the Federal Reserve at which commercial banks lend reserve balances to each other overnight. It serves as the primary benchmark for US monetary policy and influences borrowing costs across the broader economy.
A unit-based measure of change in interest rates, where one basis point equals 0.01%. A 25-basis-point hike refers to a quarter-percentage-point increase in the policy rate, commonly used to describe incremental central bank tightening decisions.
A chart published by the Federal Reserve summarising individual policymakers' anonymous projections for the future path of the federal funds rate. It is closely watched by markets as a forward guidance tool for monetary policy expectations.
A widely used measure of price-level changes tracking the cost of a fixed basket of consumer goods and services. Central banks monitor CPI readings closely when calibrating interest rate decisions relative to inflation targets.
The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, measuring changes in the prices paid by consumers for goods and services. PCE is considered broader than CPI and is the benchmark against which the Fed measures its 2% inflation target.
The annualised return on US government bonds maturing in ten years, widely used as a global risk-free rate benchmark. Elevated Treasury yields increase the relative attractiveness of dollar-denominated assets, drawing capital away from emerging markets.
US Fed keeps rates unchanged; what it means for the Indian equity market
The US Federal Reserve’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged at 3.75%-4.00% could offer limited support to Indian equities, as persistent inflation, the possibility of further monetary tightening and elevated crude oil prices continue to cloud the market outlook, according to market experts.
In an overnight development, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to maintain the benchmark federal funds rate, with two policymakers favouring a 25-basis-point hike. Although the decision was in line with market expectations, the dissenting votes highlighted a growing divide within the committee over the appropriate policy response to persistent inflation.
In its policy statement, the FOMC said economic activity was expanding at a strong pace, supported by resilient domestic spending, productivity growth and robust capital investment. Job gains had kept pace with the workforce, while the unemployment rate had changed little.
However, the central bank reiterated that inflation remained elevated and emphasised its commitment to returning inflation to its 2% target.
For Indian markets, the Fed’s stance has implications for foreign portfolio investor (FPI) flows, the rupee and equity valuations. The prospect of further US monetary tightening could keep global financial conditions restrictive, potentially limiting foreign capital inflows into emerging markets.
December rate hike in focus
Ankita Pathak, head of global investments at Ionic Asset, said the Fed’s decision to hold rates steady at its second meeting following the September 2026 rate hike reflected a calibrated, data-dependent approach.
“Overall economic growth and labour markets remain sufficiently strong, giving the US Fed time to focus on price stability for now,” she said, adding that a December rate hike appeared likely, in line with the projections in the September policy's dot plot.
Pathak noted that US inflation remained above target, with the latest consumer price index (CPI) and personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation readings at 3.7% and 3.4%, respectively. The September dot plot projected inflation returning to the Fed’s 2% target only in 2029, a year later than previously expected.
She added that US Treasury yields had softened from extremely elevated levels amid renewed safe-haven demand. Markets will now monitor policy decisions from the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan, alongside potential volatility ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
Pathak also noted that India could maintain a tighter monetary policy stance to curb inflationary pressures and rupee depreciation.
Foreign flows, bond yields in focus
Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, founder and CEO of HST Wealth, a SEBI-registered research analyst firm, said the Fed’s decision had not materially eased global financial conditions.
He pointed to the US 10-year Treasury yield, which was around 5.02% in his assessment, saying elevated yields could allow dollar assets to continue competing with emerging markets for capital. This could constrain foreign inflows into Indian equities if yields remain high.
Thomas Priju, portfolio manager at Karma Capital, said the Fed’s pause should not be interpreted as the end of the tightening cycle. Another rate increase could keep US bond yields and the dollar elevated, increasing volatility in Indian equities. High-valuation stocks and segments more dependent on foreign portfolio flows could be particularly vulnerable to changes in global liquidity.
The Fed chair also indicated that, while overall financial conditions had tightened, he was unwilling to characterise them as tight, underscoring the committee’s continued focus on inflation.
Crude oil adds to market pressure
Elevated crude oil prices remain another headwind for Indian equities. Brent crude was trading near $114.50 a barrel, while WTI crude was around $102, according to market commentary provided by analysts.
Sustained high oil prices could increase India’s import bill, pressure the rupee and raise costs for oil-sensitive sectors.
Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, expects Indian markets to remain range-bound and volatile amid global monetary policy uncertainty and geopolitical risks. He said elevated crude prices and limited progress towards diplomatic de-escalation could restrict the scope for a sustained market recovery.

articles.summary: Yen gains after BOJ holds rates, dollar slips  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
By Amanda Cooper and Chibuike Oguh
NEW YORK/LONDON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - The yen was on track for a third consecutive daily gain on Friday after the Bank of Japan left rates unchanged and upgraded its inflation outlook, while declining US Treasury yields weighed on the dollar.
The BOJ left its main rate at 1.25% in a widely anticipated move, but stressed that its policy has entered a new, more hawkish phase open to raising rates once every few months.
The yen was last up 0.11% at 157.51 per dollar, but was on track for a monthly loss in October.
"The market is a little disappointed in the BOJ," said Joseph Trevisani, senior analyst at FXStreet. "The yen is a little bit stronger today but not as strong as it has been. We still have the Fed bias countering what the BOJ is doing."
The BOJ wraps up a week of central bank decisions, with the European Central Bank, the US Federal Reserve and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand all leaving interest rates unchanged as they bide their time amid stubborn inflation and tightening financial conditions.
"We think the macroeconomic backdrop will remain sufficiently constructive for the BoJ to hike in December, March and July bringing rates to 2% before taking a pause to assess the impact of tightening," said TS Lombard analyst Rory Green in an investor note.
The euro was down 0.12% at $1.1168 and was headed for a second straight monthly loss in October. It hit its lowest since May 2025 on Thursday, after the ECB left rates unchanged and indicated higher bond yields had tightened financial conditions, initially prompting traders to lower their expectations for a hike in December.
The Bank of England and the Reserve Bank of Australia will be in focus next week.
Sterling strengthened 0.15% to $1.3396. The Australian dollar strengthened 0.09% versus the greenback to $0.70345. Both currencies were on track for an October monthly gain.
AI WORRIES
When investors seek out safe-haven assets, the dollar is often a beneficiary. But on Friday the drag from a decline in Treasury yields was stronger. Results from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel this week have rekindled worries about AI spending, which triggered a selloff in tech stocks on Friday.
The dollar index, which tracks the US currency against six others, was flat at 101.88. It is set for a second straight month of gains.
The euro has found some support from the pressure that the AI-led selloff has put on the dollar, but with euro zone economic growth lagging that of the United States, this strength may soon dissipate, according to Barclays currency strategist Lefteris Farmakis.

Alvarado said investors should focus on the path ahead as “elevated energy and other goods prices, geopolitical disruptions, and strong AI-related investment demand continue to fuel inflation pressures.”
He added, “In our view, these pressures should ultimately prompt additional Fed rate hikes and keep longer-term interest rates elevated,” while also warning that tariffs, higher borrowing costs, and fading fiscal support could make the path through 2027 bumpier.
He said those crosscurrents argue for selectivity, writing that “bumps in the road do not necessarily mean the economy is headed off course” and that he still expects resilience through 2027 as consumer spending stays buoyant and liquidity and bank lending conditions provide support. He also wrote, “Markets rarely offer investors an all-clear signal.”

Commodities, Crypto, And Global Equity Markets

articles.title: US economy grows faster than expected but inflation rises to 3.7%
articles.summary: Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loomThe US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its ad...
articles.full_text:
The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.
Estimates ranged from a 1% growth rate to a 4.2% pace.
The growth comes as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven business investment has more than offset the impact of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.
The change is in stark contrast to households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment.
The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of about 2%. New data from the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, showed that prices increased 0.5% for the month in September and the annualized inflation rate rose to 3.6%. In August, the PCE’s inflation rate was 3.4%.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to an annualized 3.1%.
The consumer price index, a separate measure of inflation released by the Department of Labor that was released earlier in October, had also shown inflation rising in September, with the annualized inflation rate going from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September.
Despite the rise in prices, the US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”.
Increasing interest rates can slow inflation, at the risk of slackening economic activity and the jobs market. Because inflation is still hot, economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December. The Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh, told reporters “economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”
Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects, in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.
Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in the second quarter. Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged behind inflation.
But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon – about $1 a gallon more than a year ago – as the US-Israel war on Iran drags on, economists anticipate a slowdown in consumer spending.
Multiple polls have shown Donald Trump’s approval rating on the economy have plummeted in the weeks before the election, with voters citing frustration over rising gas and grocery prices. Overall consumer sentiment, measured by the University of Michigan is down 15% from February, before the start of the war with Iran, as consumers expect more inflation to come.

articles.title: USD/JPY (158.28) Tests Its 200-Day Average as a Hawkish Fed Split Keeps the 275bp Carry Gap Intact - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: USD/JPY (158.28) Tests Its 200-Day Average as a Hawkish Fed Split Keeps the 275bp Carry Gap Intact  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
USD/JPY (158.28) Tests Its 200-Day Average as a Hawkish Fed Split Keeps the 275bp Carry Gap Intact
The Fed upgraded growth to “strong” and markets price 79 basis points of hikes in the year ahead | That's TradingNEWS
Key Points
- USD/JPY trades at 158.28, 26 pips below its 200-day moving average at 158.54 after the Fed decision.
- The Fed held at 3.75%–4.00% in a 10–2 vote, with Cook and Hammack dissenting for a quarter-point hike.
- Japan’s Ministry of Finance bought 11.74 trillion yen in spring intervention as USD/JPY approached 160.
USD/JPY traded at 158.28 after the Federal Reserve’s decision on Wednesday, up 0.21% on the day and 30 pips higher than its level just before the 18:00 GMT announcement. The Federal Open Market Committee held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4.00% in a 10–2 vote, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissenting in favor of an immediate quarter-point hike. The pair climbed toward 158.50 as the dollar firmed through Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference.
The yen weakened even though the Fed did nothing. Two dissents for a hike told the market that the committee’s next move, if there is one, is higher, not lower. The statement upgraded its description of economic activity from “solid” to “strong,” kept its warning that “inflation remains elevated,” and replaced its September language with a commitment to “accumulating more information” before deciding the appropriate stance. That combination is a hawkish hold, and hawkish holds widen the yield gap that drives USD/JPY.
The gap is large and stable. The Fed’s upper bound of 4.00% sits 275 basis points above the Bank of Japan’s 1.25% policy rate. After the decision, markets priced roughly 79 basis points of Fed hikes over the next year, and the US 2-year Treasury yield rose 2.7 basis points to 4.75%, touching 4.78%. Even if the BoJ hikes to 1.50% in December, as 83% of surveyed economists expect, the carry trade still pays a holder of dollars more than 2.5 percentage points a year to fund in yen.
The yen’s next catalyst arrives in less than 36 hours. The BoJ concludes its two-day meeting on Friday, October 30, with a decision around 03:00 GMT and Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference at 06:30 GMT. A hold at 1.25% is widely expected. What matters is whether the quarterly Outlook Report and Ueda’s guidance confirm a December hike.
The ceiling is Tokyo’s. Japan’s Ministry of Finance bought 11.74 trillion yen between April 28 and May 27, 2026, and Japan and the US carried out a joint intervention in July. Any move toward 160.00 risks another round. The forecast through Friday is a range between 157.00 and 159.30, with the 200-day moving average at 158.54 as the pivot and 160.00 as the line the market will not test lightly.
A Three-Day Recovery From a 156.00 One-Month Low
The pair’s move on Wednesday extended a recovery that began late last week. USD/JPY fell to the vicinity of 156.00 on Friday, October 23, its lowest level since September 18, as the yen drew support from BoJ Governor Ueda’s hawkish comments that underlying inflation is nearing the 2% target, strengthening the case for an imminent hike. Haven demand also supported the yen as US equities sold off on October 22.
The rebound started on Monday. USD/JPY attracted fresh sellers early in the week but then turned higher, gaining for three straight days. It traded above 157.00 on Tuesday and held modest gains above 157.50 on Wednesday morning as traders positioned for the Fed and the BoJ. By the time of the Fed decision, the pair stood near 157.93.
The haven bid that lifted the yen last week faded quickly. As AI-related equities recovered on Tuesday, led by semiconductors after Broadcom’s $63 billion financing deal, the risk-off demand for yen reversed. USD/JPY recovered 68% of its slide from the October 14 high to the October 23 low before the Fed decision, a sign that the late-October yen rally was driven by temporary sentiment rather than a shift in rate expectations.
The October high frames the upside. USD/JPY touched 158.95 on October 14 after a hot US inflation reading, and traded near 158.50 around October 20 on reports that the BoJ was leaning against an October rate hike. Wednesday’s post-Fed level of 158.28 sits just 67 pips below that high.
The dollar’s broader strength supported the move. The dollar index rose to a two-week high of 102.39 before the decision after a three-day rally, and the 10-year Treasury yield held at 5.01%. The dollar firmed slightly after Warsh’s press conference, with his tone supporting dollar stability rather than weakness.
The cross-yen picture shows the yen’s weakness is broad. GBP/JPY traded around 209.70 earlier Wednesday, and EUR/JPY moved lower only as the euro itself fell to its 2026 low of 1.1113 against the dollar. The yen has not been gaining against other currencies; it has been losing ground against a dollar that is backed by the highest real yields in the developed world.
A 10–2 Vote With Cook and Hammack Dissenting for a Hike
The Fed’s decision was expected, but the vote was not. The FOMC held the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00%, leaving it where it has been since September’s quarter-point increase, the first hike since 2023. Futures had priced just a 7% chance of a hike at the time of the decision. Two officials, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, preferred to raise the target range by a quarter point.
The dissents were historic. It was the first time a Fed governor and a regional bank president dissented together on the same side since October 1992, and it was Cook’s first dissent since she joined the board in 2022. Cook is also the governor President Donald Trump has tried to fire, which led some observers to describe her dissent as a possible protest vote. This was the second meeting under Warsh’s chairmanship, which began in May, to produce dissents.
The statement shifted in a hawkish direction. The description of economic activity was upgraded from “solid” to “strong.” The committee repeated that inflation remains elevated, that job gains have kept pace with workforce growth, that domestic spending has been resilient, and that productivity growth is strong and capital investment robust. The sentence saying the September action would support a more timely return of inflation to 2% was replaced with language stating that accumulating more information will help the committee determine the appropriate stance of policy.
That replacement is the key change for USD/JPY. It frames the October hold as an observational pause rather than the end of tightening. Combined with two dissents favoring higher rates and an upgraded growth assessment, the statement leaves December open and tilts the risk toward another hike.
The market reaction was measured. The S&P 500 rose 14 points, the 2-year yield climbed 2.7 basis points to 4.75%, and WTI crude rose $2.94 to $102.82. Treasury yields were broadly steady, with the 2-year rate trading around 4.76% later in the session. USD/JPY’s 30-pip gain was the largest move in the major currency pairs, reflecting the yen’s sensitivity to US rate expectations.
The political backdrop added scrutiny. The decision came six days before the US midterm elections, and some economists had warned that an unexplained hold would invite suspicion that politics drove policy. The two dissents and the hawkish statement undercut that suspicion, which helped the dollar.
Warsh: The “Monetary Medicine” Is Working, but There Is No Soft Target
Warsh’s press conference reinforced the hawkish hold. He said the overwhelming judgment of the committee was that the September hike, which removed a dose of accommodation, was starting to work, but that there were no firm conclusions. He said he was encouraged by the progress made in a short period, while acknowledging that the Fed had not yet achieved price stability.
He drew a hard line on the target. Warsh made clear there is no soft inflation target and that 2% PCE inflation remains the only objective. He stressed that relative price increases, such as the energy-driven jump in prices since the Iran war began, must not broaden into a wider inflation problem. He noted that longer-term inflation expectations still show that households and businesses trust the Fed’s commitment.
He described financial conditions as tighter but not tight. Warsh emphasized that monetary policy operates primarily through financial conditions without needing to throw sand into the gears of the economy. With the 10-year Treasury at 5.01%, financial conditions are already doing part of the Fed’s work, which is part of why the committee chose to wait.
He gave no timeline for rate cuts. Warsh’s tone was neither dovish nor hawkish on the surface, but it contained clear warnings: no rush to ease, inflation still too high, and December decided by data. That is a profile that keeps US yields sticky and supports the dollar against low-yielding currencies.
He addressed politics directly. Warsh said politics played no role in the decision, and that he did not hear a single utterance about politics in two days of meetings. That statement matters for the dollar because it protects the Fed’s credibility, which in turn supports demand for US assets.
He also announced a structural change. Warsh said the Fed will cut back on the number of meetings where members vote on rates, with a change to the FOMC schedule starting next fall. From 2028, the committee will move to six policy meetings and two meetings devoted to major economic issues, where it does not expect to make rate decisions or release statements. Fewer rate-setting meetings mean fewer scheduled opportunities to adjust policy, which could increase volatility around each remaining meeting.
The overall message for USD/JPY is that the Fed is not easing anytime soon. That keeps the 275-basis-point gap with the BoJ intact and leaves the dollar’s carry advantage untouched.
A 275bp Policy Gap and 79bp of Fed Hikes Pri

articles.full_text:
Trading vista: Higher for longer: What rising rate expectations mean for short-duration investors
Jason Graveley, Senior Manager, Fixed Income Trading
Corporate treasury professionals and fixed income investors have spent much of the past 2 years evaluating the path of Federal Reserve policy, Treasury yields and short-duration investment opportunities. Today, the conversation has shifted. Rather than debating how quickly rates may decline, investors are increasingly considering whether interest rates could remain higher for longer and potentially move higher still. While that environment presents challenges for borrowers, it may also create opportunities for cash investors and short-duration portfolios.
For much of the past 2 years, the story in rates appeared fairly straightforward. After beginning to ease in September 2024, the Fed lowered its target range from 4.75%–5.00% to 3.50%–3.75% by December 2025.3 The path was not always a straight line, but the general expectation was that policy was gradually moving back toward neutral and that additional tightening was behind us. Surely the Fed would become more accommodative? However, that narrative has shifted materially this year, not coincidentally alongside new military action in the Middle East and an abrupt spike in energy prices.
Persistent inflation, resilient economic growth and a labor market that has been slow to weaken have challenged the idea that the existing level of rates was restrictive enough to control inflation without unnecessarily weakening economic growth. In September, the Fed reversed course and raised its target range by 25 basis points (bps) to 3.75%–4.00%. What had been viewed as a gradual return toward neutral suddenly gave way to the view that tighter policy would once again be necessary to help control inflation.
As of October 13, the date of this writing, federal funds futures were pricing in the equivalent of approximately three additional 25-bps increases by mid-2027.4 Rather than debating how quickly the Fed might continue cutting toward neutral, investors are now considering whether the September increase was only the first step in a renewed series of hikes.
The move in the 2-year Treasury captures that shift as well as anything. The yield began 2026 at approximately 3.47% and reached 4.80% in October, an increase more than 130 bps year-to-date. This was roughly 140 bps above its February low of 3.38%.4 That is a meaningful reversal for a portion of the curve closely tied to the expected path of monetary policy. The market's message is no longer simply that rates may remain higher for longer. Increasingly, it's that rates may need to move higher still.
All about the data
So, what has been the key catalyst for the change in policy direction? At the very core, it has been the data. Inflation has remained persistent enough to limit the Fed's flexibility, while economic growth and labor market conditions have held up better than many expected. The combination has challenged the assumption that simply cutting rates toward neutral would be enough. Inflation doesn't necessarily need to reaccelerate sharply for this dynamic to continue. If progress toward the Fed's 2.0% objective remains slow or uneven, policymakers may have little reason to provide rate relief. And if inflationary pressures intensify, the case for additional tightening becomes more difficult to ignore.
At the same time, the economy has continued to absorb higher rates without showing the degree of deterioration many had anticipated. The labor market has remained resilient and continues to add new jobs, even if sometimes less than expected in the monthly data releases. Consumer activity has held up relatively well, and continued economic growth has provided policymakers with room to remain patient. However, this last point about resilient economic strength may also be a sign that the current policy rate is not as restrictive as previously believed or needed.
All this leads to a broader question: What if a neutral policy stance is simply higher than we've grown acclimated to? For much of the period following the global financial crisis and then reinforced by the pandemic, investors became accustomed to unusually low interest rates. But changes in inflation dynamics, fiscal policy, investment and the general structure of the economy are suggesting that the policy rate that neither stimulates nor restricts growth is now higher than it was during the last cycle. That would challenge the assumption that interest rates will naturally return to the levels that prevailed in the years before inflation reemerged. It could also help explain why the market is pricing in a higher path for policy after the Fed had already begun cutting. The market's repricing also suggests that hopes for materially lower borrowing costs may take longer to be realized.
As of October 13, federal funds futures were implying an overnight rate of approximately 4.15% by December 2026. This rises to 4.43% by March 2027 and again to 4.66% by July 2027.4 That's forecasting quite a shift higher during the first half of next year. Compared with the current implied overnight rate of approximately 3.88%, the futures curve was pricing the equivalent of about three additional 25-bps increases by mid-2027. Of course, futures pricing is not a promise that the Fed will follow that exact path. Expectations can and do change quickly, and we will have plenty of inflation, employment and growth data to mull over. Still, the shift is significant. The market has moved beyond simply removing anticipated cuts and is now assigning meaningful weight to the idea that further tightening may be necessary.
The silver lining?
Importantly, the Fed does not have to deliver every increase currently reflected in futures for short-term Treasury yields to remain elevated. Financial markets continually incorporate new information into prices and expectations, and the front end of the curve reflects the expected path of policy across multiple meetings, not simply the outcome of the next one. If the market pushes easing further into the future, raises its estimate of the peak policy rate, or concludes that the eventual policy floor will be higher, 1- to 3-year Treasury yields could remain under upward pressure. Even if the Fed ultimately delivers fewer hikes than the futures curve currently implies, an extended period of restrictive policy may be enough to keep front-end yields elevated. Put it all together and the approximately 130-bps increase in the 2-year Treasury yield reflects a broader reassessment of how high rates may need to go. It also reflects a reassessment of how long rates may remain elevated and where they may ultimately settle. And although the financial media and politicians often focus on the cost side of the equation when it comes to interest rates, for short-duration investors that shift higher is the silver lining.
In terms of portfolio construction, the risk is relatively straightforward. If the Fed tightens further, or if the market raises its expected policy path again, short-term Treasury yields could continue to rise. That would place downward pressure on the market value of existing fixed-income securities and could create additional near-term volatility. The other side of that trade-off is the increasingly attractive carry and current income potential. With the 2-year Treasury at 4.66%, investors are being paid considerably more than the beginning of the year. Higher starting yields provide more income and may offer a larger cushion against modest increases in market rates.
Short-duration maturities also give investors more frequent opportunities to reinvest. That reinvestment flexibility is particularly valuable when the direction of monetary policy remains uncertain. If yields move higher, maturing securities and available cash can be put to work at more attractive levels. If yields remain relatively stable, investors can continue collecting the attractive income currently available. And if inflation eventually moderates and the Fed can ease, short-duration holdings may still benefit from some price appreciation. Expected bouts of volatility aside, it appears to be a favorable environment for fixed income investors focused on the short end of the curve.

articles.full_text:
(Kitco News) – The Federal Reserve announced on Wednesday that the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 in favor of maintaining the policy rate unchanged, as expected by the market consensus.
“The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate,” the Federal Reserve said in its statement. “The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.”
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the statement read. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”
The central bank warned, however, that inflation remains elevated. “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal,” they said. “The Committee will deliver price stability.”
FOMC members Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack voted against the monetary policy action and the statement, both preferring to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at Wednesday's meeting.
The Fed statement did not include any guidance about future rate moves.
Gold prices dropped in the wake of the announcement, with spot gold last trading at $4,035.48 per ounce for a loss of 0.60% on the session.
Chris Zaccarelli, Chief Investment Officer of Northlight Asset Management, said the Fed left plenty of clues that they were planning to raise rates in December.
"As always, a lot can change in the data between now and then, but if it weren’t so close to the midterm elections, they probably would have raised rates today, and now it’s unlikely that anything will stop them from raising rates at the next meeting," he said. "Next year, the picture is less clear. The futures are predicting two more rate hikes, and that makes sense if everything stays the same, but as we have learned over the past couple of years, things rarely do (e.g. tariffs, Iran war, etc)."
Zaccarelli expects the economy to sufffer as rates move higher and the AI buildout is impacted. "If we have a growth slowdown or recession in the next 12 months, then of course the Fed will react and we will see lower interest rates by the end of next year, but if the economy continues to be resilient despite all of the macroeconomic headwinds, then the Fed may end up raising even more than the 2 times that are currently priced in."
