articles.title: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test - The Verge
articles.summary: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test  The VergeRivian Says the R2 Is Outselling the R1T Truck, R1S SUV, and Its Delivery Vans Combined  Car and DriverRivian's stock correction allows favorable 'entry point' after Q3 earnings, Jefferies says  CNBCR2 becomes Rivian’s top seller as construction progresses at $5B Georgia plant  The Atlanta Journal-ConstitutionRivian rallies on strong EV sales  Los Angeles Times
articles.full_text:
During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company’s still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions.
Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
RJ Scaringe spent nearly half of Rivian’s earnings call hyping self-driving tech. But taking on Tesla’s FSD with custom chips and pricey lidar is an enormous gamble while the mass-market R2 is still scaling up.
But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027. Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028. In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player.
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator,” Derek Mulvey, VP for finance, said during the call.
Success is not guaranteed. Tesla has a huge head start with its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in over 1.7 million active customer cars. But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.)
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.”
— Derek Mulvey
But it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider. That leaves the company in the middle of a difficult balancing act: launching an ambitious, mass-market electric vehicle while simultaneously reinventing itself as a full-stack autonomous driving powerhouse.
Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed. During the call, Scaringe revealed that he has been using the new point-to-point driving system in his own commute to the office every day, calling it “a wonderful” experience. He continued:
So, our view is that that is going to become a big driver of demand. And I think it’s unclear how quickly the whole — you know, the whole US market and the whole automotive market — starts to shift to really wanting this, and this being a major purchase criterion. But certainly, we’re at the front end of an inflection point where it’s more and more people exposed to what this could do… We do think it’s a really big driver, in the long term, for market share for us.
But Scaringe was cagey about other details. When asked about Rivian’s take rate for its Autonomy Plus package — in other words, what percentage of Rivian buyers who purchase or subscribe to the software out of the total customer base — the chief executive declined to share the exact number. “The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.”
Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported. Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year. And Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin.
Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems. On the call, the company pointed out that computer chips, memory, and electronics are getting pricier. It also warned that adding two processors and costly lidar sensors to some R2 models could eat into the profits it hoped to make by building the vehicle in large numbers.
The point-to-point system will face its own hurdles, including edge cases and the complexities of urban driving. A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD. And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong.
To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo. Self-driving tech could help Rivian post big, software-company-style profits, but paying for expensive AI development while also trying to build the R2 at scale makes the next year or two its riskiest period ever.

articles.title: Philip R. Lane: AI adoption in Europe
articles.full_text:
- SPEECH
AI adoption in Europe
Keynote speech by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Research Symposium on AI and the economy
San Francisco, 30 October 2026
My aim today is to describe how AI is reshaping the euro area economy.[1] Although the development of frontier AI models is primarily taking place in the United States and China, the adoption of AI will be a key determinant of European productivity growth in the coming years, while expenditure on AI adoption also currently constitutes a significant stimulus to the euro area economy.[2] In addition, European firms are part of the global AI supply chain, while European investors are contributing to the funding of the global buildout of AI infrastructure through equity and debt markets and the banking system.
I will also describe the key patterns we see in the data, with a primary focus on how the surveys conducted by the ECB can provide insights into the AI adoption process and the implications for the financial system.[3][4]
Aggregate trends
Digital investment in the euro area has expanded by 73 per cent in real terms since 2014, increasing from 2.3 per cent to 3.3 per cent of GDP (Chart 1a). While digital investment has grown far more quickly in the United States, the surge in digital investment (with an estimated clear acceleration since 2024) marks a distinct shift in the structure of the euro area economy.[5] As shown in Chart 1b, in the euro area digital investment has primarily been in intangible assets, while investment in data centres has constituted a relatively small share.[6]
Chart 1
Digital investment in the euro area
| a) Digital investment proxy, euro area | b) Digital investment proxy, euro area, with asset breakdown | 
|---|---|
| (2014 = 100) | (EUR billion) | 
| Sources: Eurostat, ECB and ECB calculations. Notes: Chart 1a shows the digital proxy for the euro area business economy, at constant 2020 prices, indexed to 2014. The blue dots for 2025 and 2026 extend the digital investment proxy based on the annual growth of an output proxy for digital services (weighted non-seasonally adjusted production of publishing activities; computer programming, consultancy and related activities; and information service activities). Chart 1b shows a digital proxy which refers to (i) investment in non-residential buildings and structures in the information and communication sector, (ii) information and communication technology (ICT) equipment in the business economy, (iii) investment in computer software and databases (CSDBs) in the business economy, excluding the ICT sector, and (iv) total intellectual property products (IPP) investment (in CSDBs and research and development) by the ICT sector. Missing country values are estimated based on known euro area aggregates of country-sector shares. On a whole-economy basis, digital investment has increased from around 2.3 per cent of euro area GDP in 2014 to 3.0 per cent in 2024 (and looks to have increased to 3.3 per cent by the end of the first half of 2026, on the basis of updates of digital services output). The latest observations are for 2024 for euro area annual accounts and July 2026 for euro area production data. |  | 
In the ECB Corporate Telephone Survey, firms report that AI has added about 10 per cent to their capital expenditure plans this year. AI-related demand has helped activity to hold up over the last two years – as reflected by the contributions of the “computers and other electronics” and “information and communication services” sectors to total market production (Chart 2a). As illustrated in Chart 2b, Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) indicators show that output, employment and new orders have developed considerably more favourably in the technology equipment subsector than in other manufacturing subsectors. For services, the software subsector has performed better than other services sectors in terms of output, albeit not in terms of employment and new orders.
Chart 2
Effects of the global AI boom on euro area output
| a) Total market production | b) PMIs for technology equipment and software in manufacturing and services | 
|---|---|
| (cumulated changes since January 2025 in per cent) | (diffusion indices, average January-September 2026) | 
| Sources: Eurostat and ECB calculations Note: The latest observations are for July 2026. | Sources: S&P Global and ECB calculations. Notes: Sectoral labels are taken from the July Global PMI press release. The latest observations are for September 2026. | 
AI has been the main driver of global goods trade over the last year (Chart 3a). European firms are contributors to the global AI supply chain. Table 4 shows that AI-related exports and imports are growing quickly in the euro area, especially in relation to core data centre goods, which contain directly deployed hardware components related to AI compute, storage and networking capacity. Possibly related to differences in composition, the increase in AI import prices in the euro area is more muted than for the other major economic regions (Chart 3b). Chart 5 shows that, while AI-related price increases have contributed materially to the upward shift in goods inflation, the impact on headline inflation is limited owing to the relatively low weight of AI-exposed goods in the consumer price index (13.3 per cent in the non-energy industrial goods subcomponent and 3.4 per cent of the HICP).
Chart 3
Trade in goods and import prices of AI goods
| a) Global goods imports by category | b) Import prices of AI goods | 
|---|---|
| (annual percentage changes, percentage points; de-meaned) | (annual percentage changes, three-month moving averages) | 
| Sources: Trade Data Monitor and ECB staff calculations. Notes: The figures are nominal data. Values are deviations from their respective mean over 2019-2023. “AI-related” reflects a basket of goods related to the construction and operation of AI data centres estimated by Emter et al. (2026) following Waugh (2026). The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. | Sources: Trade Data Monitor, ECB and ECB staff calculations. Notes: Import prices are calculated as unit values. “AI goods” is a basket of goods related to AI data centre construction (Emter et al. 2026; Waugh 2026). Unless otherwise indicated, prices are in US dollars. “Asia – AI exporters” includes Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the Philippines. The latest observations are for July 2026 for the euro area, Asia and Global, August 2026 for the United States and September 2026 for China. | 
Table 4
Trade in AI goods
| Trade in AI-related goods and subcomponents | 
|---|
| Sources: Eurostat, Trade Data Monitor and ECB staff calculations. Notes: The table shows the share and growth in values. Rest of the world refers to the world excluding the euro area and the United States. 2023 shares are the shares of imports/exports in total imports/exports of the respective country or region. “AI-related trade” refers to goods related to the construction and operation of AI data centres (Emter et al., 2026; Waugh, 2026). “Core data centre goods” are directly deployed hardware components related to AI compute, storage, and networking capacity. “Data centre infrastructure goods” are physical infrastructure goods required to power, cool, and operate data centre facilities. “Other AI-related goods” are upstream AI goods and broad industrial goods used in AI production. | 
Chart 5
Price pressures from rising prices for AI goods
| a) Consumer product exposure to AI goods | b) HICP weights of AI-exposed goods | 
|---|---|
| (percentage of output) | (percentage points) | 
| Sources: Trade Data Monitor, BEA (US Bureau of Economic Analysis), Eurostat and ECB staff calculations. Notes: “AI goods” is a basket of goods related to AI data centre construction (Emter et al. 2026; Waugh, 2026). The data are based on US BEA tables (2017). Exposures are weighted by AI share, based on 2025 nominal trade data. | Sources: Eurostat and ECB staff calculations. Note: HICP weights in 2026. | 
In relation to trade in services, Chart 6 shows a significant upward movement in software licence imports from the United States since 2022, consistent with increased purchasing of AI licences from the leading US firms.[7]
Chart 6
Euro area intellectual property products imports
| Euro area payments for the use of intellectual property products (imports) | 
|---|
| Sources: ECB (euro area balance of payments), BEA (US Bureau of Economic Analysis, US trade in services) and ECB staff calculations. Notes: Euro area charges for the use of intellectual property (imports) are based on quarterly ECB balance of payments data. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. Imports from the United States are broken down by type of intellectual property using annual shares by type in US exports to the euro area, as reported by the BEA (mirror data). These shares are applied to quarterly euro area imports of intellectual property from the United States for the corresponding year. The latest available BEA data refer to 2025; the 2025 shares are also applied to 2026 quarters. | 
European investors are also major purchasers of US technology-related equities (Chart 7). Listed European tech firms have also benefited from rising stock market valuations (Chart 8a). Stock returns, revenue growth, operating margin growth and earnings per share growth are all increasing in AI-intensity (Chart 8b).
Chart 7
Euro area purchases of US shares

articles.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17bn in major grocery delivery consolidation
articles.summary: Acquisition will supercharge DoorDash’s grocery delivery, ‘one of the hardest things to get right online’, CEO saysDoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. articles.full_text:
DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.
DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.
Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the US and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” – who are independent contractors – completed 338m orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14bn.
DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3bn orders last year using a network of 9m independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73bn.
DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.
The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 US Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco .
Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.
“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”
DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on US delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.
It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.
